text:
I’m Korean, born and raised in this country, and after watching this video, I just sat in silence for a while. Not because it shocked me, but because it said out loud what so many of us already feel deep inside: that it’s too late. There’s no fixing this anymore.

I’m in my early 30s now, living in Seoul, working a job that consumes most of my time and energy. I went to a good university, did everything “right” according to our society’s standards, but I feel like I’m running on empty. Every day feels like survival, not life.

Korea’s government throws money at us — baby bonuses, housing incentives, free childcare. But it all feels like putting a tiny bandage on a broken system. No amount of money can fix the reality we live in. The pressure to succeed starts when you're a toddler and never ends. Our school system is brutal. Our work culture glorifies sacrifice and burnout. Taking a break is seen as weakness. Saying “no” is disrespectful. You grow up being told that your worth is based on your productivity.

Marriage? Kids? They’re not even dreams anymore — they’re burdens. My friends and I talk more about escaping the country than building a family. Who wants to bring a child into a world where they’ll suffer the same way we did, or worse?

And honestly, we’re tired of pretending we’re okay. We’re tired of being told that it’s our “duty” to save the nation by having children when the nation never cared about our well-being in the first place. We didn’t get affordable housing, fair jobs, or mental health support — but now we’re expected to sacrifice for the next generation?

The saddest part is that even those who want to have kids feel they can’t. Not in this environment. Not with these expectations. People say “maybe things will get better,” but how? Korea has had decades to change, and instead it doubled down on competition, image, and control.

I love my country, but I don’t trust it anymore. The gap between the people and the policymakers is too wide. The policies are written by older men who never lived like us, never felt this hopelessness. And by the time real change could come — if it ever does — it’ll be too late.

This isn’t just a crisis of numbers. It’s a crisis of spirit. We’re not just disappearing in population — we’re disappearing in hope

The ironic thing here is that the school is actively encouraging insane studying hours (i wake up at 6 a.m. and school technically ends at 4 p.m, but after that we have extracurriculars and nocturnal study, and i come back home at least past 11 p.m.) while also insisting that we get proper amounts of sleep. There's a lot of pressure on getting into a good university too (if it's not SKY, you're a failure, is the general consensus of the teachers). I've seen graduates retake the equivalent of the SATs here multiple times even though they've already gotten into a decent university.

From what the adults tell me, it's like your life peaks at what university you get into, and they don't teach us about anything else beyond that. And it's really funny that the only thing my school (a very expensive private one) has to be proud of is the amount of students they send to Seoul University every year, and not its facilities or amount of care they provide students with. My friend on the student council says that the school cut the funding for the council this year. It might just be my opinion, but to me it seems that the school (and system in general) doesn't view students as people at all, they're only methods to maintain their so-called prestige.

+ edit: i forgot to mention that the majority of the students here all suffer from some sort of caffeine addiction, joint pains, sleep deprivation, or some other kind of pain, and all the school tells us is 'it gets better once you get into college' :)

text:
I’m Korean, and I’m currently living in Australia. The moment I arrived, I felt it.
“This is the real world.”
For the first time, I saw what it means for people to actually live — not just exist.

I had always known, at least intellectually, that Korea was a high-pressure society and that Western countries seemed more relaxed and happy. But nothing could’ve prepared me for the difference between knowing it through a screen and witnessing it with my own eyes.

Here in Australia, at any hour of the day, you see adults enjoying a quiet coffee, teenagers laughing while playing catch on a field, and children running freely with large dogs by their side. It looked like a scene from a film — and yet, it was real. That’s what stunned me the most.
But what really hit me was the sudden realization that I had never seen anything like this in my own country. Why did this feel so unfamiliar, so distant — almost impossible? Why did this simple, peaceful life feel like fiction to me?

That’s when I understood:
I hadn’t been living. I had been surviving.

Back in high school, I spent every day at school from 7:30 a.m. to 10 p.m. And after that, I went to private academies to study even more. To you, that might sound extreme — but in Korea, this is as normal as Australians lying in the park for an afternoon nap.
It’s not an exception. It’s the rule.
We weren’t living human lives. We were functioning like machines.

But the truth is — we’re not machines.
And no human can endure a machine’s life forever.

In Korea, being “enough” means being perfect. Not just in appearance — but in school, in work, in relationships, in personality, in every aspect of life. It’s a society that demands flawlessness, yet offers no room to breathe.

And the scariest part?
We all accept it.
We’re all caught in a system where everyone is both a victim and a contributor. We compete, we compare, we push — and we break.

Meanwhile, Australians seem to live differently. They live with ease, with presence, with self-acceptance. They don’t rush to become something more; they simply are.

As someone who grew up in Korea, it pains me to say this — but the everyday peace I witness here feels less real to me than ‘Squid Game’ ever did.

Of course, Korea has its own rhythm — fast, vibrant, full of stimulation and drama you can’t find anywhere else.
And yes, sometimes Australia feels almost too quiet. Too slow. Too still. Honestly, it’s boring.

But maybe that’s the point.
Maybe we’ve mistaken chaos for meaning,
and stimulation for life.

Because in Korea, we chase impossible ideals — academic success, perfect careers, flawless looks, ideal love, social approval — all at once, all the time. We’ve built a society that demands more than humans can give.

And now, we face the consequences:
a country heading toward extinction not through war, but through burnout.
A society where people no longer choose to bring life into the world, because they’re too busy surviving their own.

text:
I’m Korean, and I didn’t cry watching this. I just went quiet — because it didn’t feel like a warning. It felt like a documentary of a country that already died, and we’re just living in its ghost.

People outside think we’re obsessed with success.
No. We’re obsessed with not failing — because here, failure doesn’t mean starting over. It means social death.
You vanish from the system. From your family’s pride. From your own identity.
We don’t live for dreams. We live to avoid shame.

I’m in my 30s. No kids. No plans for marriage. Not because I’m bitter or selfish — but because I know exactly what I’d be handing to a child. A life where rest feels illegal.
Where happiness is a side quest, not the goal.
Where love is transactional.
Where every decision is a calculation:
“Will this make me more efficient? More impressive? More acceptable?”

The truth is: we don’t fear being alone. We fear being seen as lazy.
We fear slowing down.
We fear not performing.

And the saddest part? We’re good at it.
We’ve mastered the art of looking fine while breaking down.
Of smiling in group photos and crying in bathrooms.
Of calling burnout “ambition.”

Yes, Korea is modern. Efficient. Clean. Safe.
But none of that matters when you start to feel like a cog in a beautiful machine — one that never turns off, never slows down, and never lets you ask “why.”

Foreigners come here and admire the order. The speed. The innovation.
But they don’t see the 3 a.m. cram schools.
The unpaid overtime masked as loyalty.
The antidepressants swallowed quietly before morning meetings.
The couples getting married just to keep up appearances.
The parents begging their kids to be “happy,” while forcing them down the same path that made them miserable.

Sometimes I wonder — what would it even look like if we just stopped?
If we let go of the image, the metrics, the constant comparisons?
Would there be anything left?

People might read this and think I’m exaggerating.
Others will read this and feel like I just opened a door they’ve been scared to admit exists.

As a korean, I can say that while everyone understands the gravity of the situation,
 the elderly and baby boomers are draining the younger generation, making any resolution nearly impossible.

In Korea’s political and social structure, young people are ignored and treated like inexperienced children, making the idea of young politicians almost unthinkable. 
As a result, all politicians are in their 50s or 60s, creating policies that only cater to the older generation, which holds the most voting power.

This tradition has continued since the founding of modern Korea, making laws and social structures that exploit the youth feel natural.

Now, with 69-hour workweeks, excessive pension extractions, and malicious conscription, the younger generation is being squeezed dry, leaving no room for new lives to be born.

"Old soldiers never die, they simply fade away.
But the system they created will neither die nor disappear."

Now, we are all marching toward doom

"Sing elder, sing of brief delight, and of youth's despair"

To provide some additional context, South Koreans are required to pay four types of social service-related taxes. Among these, the national pension and health insurance systems are projected to be depleted due to population decline — the pension fund by 2055 and health insurance by 2028.

Of course, we understand the importance of these policies and recognize the need to support the older generation who built the foundation of our society. However, in the face of this impending depletion, the government’s response has not been reform for the future. Instead, it has chosen to maintain a structure where young people pay more while the elderly receive more.

This approach essentially fuels division between generations, embodying the idea of “divide and rule.” A society that chooses division over unity ends up fostering hostility — between the young and the old, between men and women — and ultimately reinforces a cynical, fractured social atmosphere.

I hope that in your country, you can dream of happiness, not exploitation.

Why aren’t Koreans having children? It is because they are finally feeling the harsh reality of income inequality based on capital and lineage that is deeply entrenched in the Western world (Europe, Canada, the United States, and the United Kingdom). They are beginning to realize that unless they are naturally gifted in academics or business, the kind of parents they have will determine their entire life, relegating them to the working class.”

In Europe, traces of monarchy remain, and the U.S. and Canada have had a capital-based class structure since the late 1800s. As a result, it’s very difficult to accumulate real wealth later. While finance jobs (e.g., private equity, investment banking) can yield high incomes, they are extremely hard to break into.

You could also make a decent living through fields like economics or computer science without necessarily going into medicine, dentistry, or law.
Today: The earnings of medical, dental, and legal professionals have outpaced other fields, and admission scores have risen so drastically that only about 8,600 out of 450,000 test-takers are accepted. 
Parental wealth—especially for private tutoring—has become a crucial factor. Without such financial backing, it’s nearly impossible to get in unless you possess exceptional natural talent.
In the past, Koreans firmly believed that anyone could succeed through hard work, regardless of financial background. text:
As a 19-year-old student living in Korea, I feel that one of the biggest problems here is the pressure to follow a fixed path from a very young age. Even before we understand who we are or what truly makes us happy, we are forced to answer questions like “What do you want to become?” — but in reality, it only means “Which university major will you choose?” In Korea, the word “dream” is just another name for “career path,” and “career path” is just about picking a department at college.

If you step off the set path, society makes you feel like you’re falling behind, like you’re somehow less than others. As students, we are always expected to be outstanding — if we’re not, we’re seen as failures. With endless exams, assignments, competitions, and the constant need to build up our academic profiles, even a moment of exhaustion or a single mistake makes us feel like we’re not good enough. It feels as though we are never allowed to rest, because any pause could mean you’re “failing” at life.

Most students I know feel trapped by the Korean education system every single day. And yet, we keep pushing ourselves because we know this is the only way to endure in this society. But university is just the beginning — after that comes the pressure of employment, then marriage, and so on. It feels like we’re always running, always being chased by something invisible. And when life feels this exhausting before it even begins, I sometimes wonder: how could we be expected to bring new life into a world that never gives us room to breathe?

Before I’ve even had the chance to ask myself, “What kind of person do I want to become?” or “Are the rules of this world truly just?” — I find myself already caught in the race. And deep down, I wonder if I ever truly had the strength to follow all the steps this society expects of me.

text:
I’m a university student in my early twenties from South Korea.
I’m not very good at English, but with the help of translation, I’d like to share my thoughts.

South Korea, once one of the poorest countries in the world, was built up solely through the unity and sacrifice of its people. But today, the politicians in power divide the people to protect their own interests, pitting them against each other for votes and influence. Korea is now fractured — split by generation, gender, religion, and countless other lines. It is, quite literally, falling apart.

Korea is a small country. 
It claims to be a liberal democracy, yet in practice, every citizen is kept under tight societal control. Basic education is free and universal, and higher education is treated almost as a social obligation. The recent university enrollment rate stands at 75%. That means 7 out of 10 people in their 20s and 30s you meet on the street have a college degree.

Most young people have studied hard, built solid careers, and gained skills that should never be underestimated — and yet, they can’t find jobs. The expectations are high, but there’s simply no meaningful work available. Imagine a top 10% physics student taking a minimum wage job serving fried chicken. But if you fall behind in the career race, what other real choices do you have?

So, even after graduating from good schools, many young Koreans pursue master’s or doctoral degrees, or enter vocational programs to boost their chances of landing a better job. They keep studying throughout their twenties, and by the time they finally get their first job in their thirties, they’re faced with another harsh reality:
To buy an average apartment in Seoul — which costs 1.3 billion won — they would need to save 30 years’ worth of the national average annual income (43 million won). And since most people and jobs are concentrated in Seoul, moving elsewhere isn’t really an option. Over 43% of households in Korea do not own a home.
It’s not an exaggeration to say that many people may never be able to afford a place to live.
And with all this... how are we supposed to have children?
I can't bear the thought of my child growing up in a world full of struggle.

Korea is aging — and with age comes inertia, dragging us further toward decline.
Politicians often implement policies that place a heavier burden on the younger generation in order to maintain support for aging populations — a structural dilemma that continues to deepen.

A good example of this is Korea’s national pension system. Recently, in the name of “sustainability,” the government increased the mandatory pension contributions taken from the wages of the younger generation by 4%, while increasing pension payouts for current retirees by 3%. Ironically, the national pension fund is projected to be depleted by 2064 — just around the time I’d be old enough to receive it. But by then, there will be nothing left.

text:
I’m a South Korean woman in my thirties currently living in Japan. Honestly, if I were still in Korea, I doubt I would have decided to have children. Japan, too, is experiencing low birth rates and an aging society, but wherever you go, you can still see children, and most households seem to have at least two.

In contrast, whenever I go to Korea for business, I rarely see any children. I was especially shocked recently when I read a news article saying that my old school, located in a densely populated area of Seoul, was closing down due to a lack of students.

While I think Korea is relatively stable, both economically and environmentally, I’m not sure if young people there truly have the means to raise kids. After enduring fierce competition to enter the job market, securing a position, and then following the ‘expected timeline’ of marriage and parenting, I’m not convinced that this process necessarily guarantees real happiness for myself or for any future child.

Additionally, prices keep rising, global resources are scarce, and international affairs remain unstable. Society’s perception of balancing work and childcare isn’t very supportive, and private education costs continue to climb. People seem to harbor mutual animosity, which politicians often exploit, and the expense of buying a house and raising kids has skyrocketed. In a country where you might be forced to retire by age 48 after studying and working hard for 25 years, I wonder how many young people can bear such a heavy burden—or would want to pass that burden on to their children.

It’s bittersweet, but I left Korea ten years ago, and as time goes on, I feel more convinced that I made the right choice. Even so, I truly wish the best for all the young people living in Korea.

text:
As a British expat who lived and worked in South Korea for four years, this video really hits home. I moved to Korea to teach English (earning around 3.1 million Korean won (around 2k USD / £1.6k) a month with free housing, which is a comfortable income) and I truly loved many aspects of living there. I made amazing friends, both Korean and foreign, and got to experience the rich culture and hospitality that Korea is known for. However, by the time I left in 2025, I had a growing feeling that the country was declining in some important ways for everyday people, myself included. This isn’t something I say lightly – it’s based on what I saw and felt during my time there.

Working at a private hagwon (academy), I saw firsthand how intense the education system is. Parents poured so much money and energy into their children’s schooling, from regular school to endless after-school academies. Even very young kids had schedules that would make most adults exhausted. I remember feeling sorry for both the children (who often looked tired and stressed) and their parents, who were sacrificing finances and personal time in hopes of securing their kid’s success. It made me understand why the birth rate in Korea is so low these days – raising even one child under these conditions requires huge dedication and resources. The pressure for kids to perform well is immense, driven by a societal belief that top-tier education is the only path to a good life. That environment didn’t seem sustainable or healthy to me in the long run, and it was heartbreaking to see the toll it took on families.

The Korean work culture was another thing that really wore me down. In Korea the expectation was that you give 110% all the time, no matter what. Breaks were almost non-existent during the workday, and there was this unspoken rule that you should stay as long as your boss stays, even if you’ve finished your tasks. I noticed people rarely took sick days. In fact, coming to work even when you’re ill was basically normal – a stark contrast to back home in the UK, where if you’re sick you take time off to recover (and it’s not seen as a lack of dedication). Over time, I felt drained by this routine. Everyone worked incredibly hard, but there was little sense of balance or time to recharge. Life seemed to revolve around work and obligations without any real pauses, which eventually started affecting my own mental and physical health.

While I, as a foreigner, was somewhat shielded from direct social expectations, I saw my Korean friends struggling with heavy societal pressures, especially as they hit their late 20s and 30s. There’s a common expectation that by a certain age you should have a stable, high-status job, get married, and then quickly have kids. text:
며칠 전, 대한민국 국회는 연금제도를 개혁하자는 법안을 통과시켰습니다. 그러나 이 법안은 젊은이들이 내는 금액을 높이면서, 노인들이 받게 되는 연금액을 그 이상 올려버렸습니다. 일부 젊은 의원들이 반대표를 던졌지만, 이 법안은 집권당과 반대편 정당을 포함해서 180명이 넘는 찬성표를 받아 통과되고 말았습니다. 심지어 일부 의원들은 노인들이 받는 금액을 더 올려야 한다고 주장했습니다.

대한민국 국민 대다수가 이 영상이 다룬 인구문제에 대해 알고 있습니다. 하지만 자기 세대가 그 값을 치르기를 거부합니다. 특히 인구가 많은 베이비 붐 세대의 경우 인구 자체가 권력이 되어 자기 세대가 내야 할 값을 자녀 세대에게 전가하고 있습니다. 입법부에서 심도있게 이 문제를 다루고 싶어해도, 입법부를 구성하는 의원들 대다수가 베이비 붐 세대입니다. 결국 모두가 문제가 무엇인지 알지만, 자기가 비용을 지불하기 싫다는 이기심 때문에 그 비용을 계속 다음 세대에게 넘기고 있습니다.

대한민국의 정치인들이 이것을 방치하는 이유는 무엇일까요? 그들 역시 베이비 붐 세대이며 은퇴가 얼마 남지 않았기 때문입니다. 그들은 자신이 죽기 전에 연금 고갈을 보지 않을 것이라고 굳게 믿고 있습니다. 또 연금이 고갈되더라도 자신은 이미 죽거나 은퇴했기 때문에, 연금 문제를 방치한 행동에 대해 평가를 받지 않습니다. 연금 고갈을 막기 위한 조치는 결국 "젊은이들이 더 많이 내거나", "노인들이 더 적게 받는" 방법밖에 없습니다. 하지만 베이비 붐 세대 의원들은 자기들이 연금을 내는 수십 년의 기간 동안 2008년 이후 단 한 번도 대책을 내지 않다가, 은퇴 직전에 이르러 젊은이들에게 더 많은 짐을 지우고 자신들이 값을 더 가져가는 결정을 내리고 말았습니다.

대한민국은 민주주의 국가입니다. 그래서 대통령도 의원도 다수의 지지를 받는 사람이 선출됩니다. 그러나, 다수의 이익이 나라의 이익과 충돌하게 되면 문제가 심각해집니다. 나라의 미래를 팔아서 자기 세대가 더 부유해지겠다는 결정을 다수의 이름으로 정당화합니다. 그리고 다수의 지지를 받아 선출된 지도자들도 그들의 이기심에 부응하기 위해 명백하게 보이는 문제점을 회피하거나 방치합니다. 이 악순환을 끊을 방법은 무엇일까요? 정말 궁금합니다

text:
I left Korea 6 years ago and have been living in Australia since. One thing I’ve come to realise here is that the root cause of the extreme competition among young children in Korea stems from the undervaluing of certain types of labour.
Some jobs are simply not paid what they deserve, and on top of that, there’s a deeply ingrained societal bias about which kinds of work are considered more ‘worthy’ or respectable.

When you think about how society functions, it simply cannot survive without what’s often referred to as the “working class” people in trades, services and manual labour. These roles are as equally important as so called "전문직“ and should be respected equally, as they form the backbone of any functioning society.

However, the Korean education system fails to teach children this reality. Instead, it reinforces the idea that only certain career paths (mainly white-collar professions) are valuable. It’s not uncommon to hear teachers say things like, "If you don’t study hard, you’ll end up digging concrete" or "You’ll be washing dishes for the rest of your life". These statements not only disrespect honest work but also instil shame around certain professions, creating a rigid hierarchy of jobs in young people’s minds.

As a result, children grow up internalising this mindset, living in fear of falling behind even before they’ve had the chance to discover who they are or what they truly want in life. This pressure pushes them into relentless competition with their peers, leading to widespread mental and physical exhaustion. It also contributes to broader cultural issues, such as the stigma around vocational education and the undervaluing of skilled trades.

Let the children breathe, play and be pure just like they deserve, and let them naturally find their own way when it's time to do so without giving them unbearable stress and suffering.

​@JimmyMon666  that's probably the case in SK as well, but it unfortunately doesn't change the indoctrination in school and society. Instead 70% of young people still go to university and not vocational training, studying in hopes of a higher paying job only to land in offices with a 9 to 9 job.  Thinking they have done everything by book to become a worker with decent pay, but unfortunately having become just one of the exploited masses that cramps into the big cities. Not enough time to date, not enough money to get kids, not enough trust in society that it will be better for their kids. IMO the government should try to bring some of the working spaces (also big companies) into the rural areas, where there's enough space for families and childfriendly places, less competition for workspace, and by the spirits vocational jobs need to be promoted a lot better to the parents - which unfortunately have a lot of say in what their kids should pursue. Vocational jobs getting more expensive is not enough to change its image of invaluable, lower jobs that you shouldn't strive for. At least it's not changing quick enough. Tbh i would even argue for a  mandatory summer/year after school where everyone has to work in a vocation. That would give the students some break from the competitiveness in the education system, and perhaps show them that there's a state of fullfilledness and contentness that comes with working with your own hands and having a finished product at the end of the day not only a turned off screen. Perhaps that would a) bring in some necessary foundational workers, and b) some purpose and appreciation in a few young people for these jobs
... sorry for the rambling, having spent some months in sk and seeing the students and young people has made me a bit passionate about the topic

text:
As a Korean, thank you for making this video - hoping at least one more people notice this.
I'm high school 3th grade student, which called most painful school age in Korea.
For example, we are to busy to study so if someone is sick during this period, it can be the 'vice'. So we have to control our health for exams. It would had to be better if we studied something great, but all our society want for us is self-mechanization which requires only a lot of solving problems to solve problems more quickely and accurately rather than deliberate thinking, sharing thoughts with others and finding dreams.
In addition, realistically we have no times to think about this problem and social atmosphere even don't give us chances to talk about this. (I think I'm fortunate cause' I'm in envirinment to think about this- even if it's hard)
If I talk this to someone(school teacher, academy teacher even friends or parents), their responce will be at best "I understand your opinion, but there is noting you can do - just study nowtime", at worst "Why you are thinking about something else? Go study. Stop imagining something useless."
The sadder fact is that the above is true and I can understand that they are speaking for us to some extent.
But, but.. If adults can only answer like this and If student have no choice but to keep hearing these answers, who will change this and when this will be changed?
I think if there is no 'dramatic' revolution, All of us but the rich will be drowned by ourselves and our society.
Thx for reading, as I said there is almost no people to say this, so I told many words here.

They expect him to land a high-paying job, get married to a Korean woman,  buy a nice apartment flat or house, have children, and take care of his parents. So much pressure that he left South Korea and enrolled at the university in Denmark, studying psychology. Fortunately, he met a wonderful Danish woman and fell in love. His family wasn't too happy about him staying in Denmark and having a "non-Korean" girlfriend.

Do not try to make a deal with the government with your already dead family, get over it, and shut your mouth about making commemorative space in the park. You victim families are disgrace to our society."
I guarantee I heard this kind of truck-speeches until like 3 years ago. To be honest, I hate this country.

text: What I learned about South-Korea by a good friend from Busan is that your "shell" is more important than your "core". Like... what kind of soul you have and how good you try to be as a human is just second to the general society standards... your looks, your skin, your eyes, your teeth etc. are more important - and also the prestige level of your education of course. How you shine to the world is number one priority. Most people don't even like that but everyone goes with the flow. On one side this attitude as a base made South-Korea to easily the cleanest and most modern industrial country in the world... it's not like in the USA, in Europe or even Southeast-Asia that you have loads of (teenager) crimes, problems with graffiti or stuff like that. You can sit, go and look everywhere without problems of safety or impurities - even big cities are clean, extremely well managed and maintained and you have the most modern technology for basically every area of ​​activity. On the other side South-Korea is damned with the worldwide highest suicide rate, very bad mobbing statistics for schools, colleges and companies and a very critical rate of people in debth (because of trying to always have the most modern and expensive things, which is hard to do even when having a well paid job). Also the wide spread of plastic surgery and the public urge to change your visuals is extremely concerning, especially because it always stands in connection with the before mentioned mobbing, suicide rate etc. - and even high ranked employees are not immune to that. And all those high standards can be seen in every working field, every niche, all types of media and entertainment - K-POP f.e. is beside of the music a big, big act of this "false perfectionism". But in the end from what I've seen is that South-Koreans (especially the youngest generations) are getting more and more away from these insane society standards, but it's def. still a long journey. A beautiful country with so many smart people and a lot of values and things that I personally would def. love to see in the western world (at leats to a certain extend) - but nothing is perfect and the more a society is built on "perfectionism", the more problems are coming with that.

text:
I lived in South Korea for two years teaching, and I can't stress enough how much it is an open secret the chaebols are the ones really running the country. Literally, everyone I would talk to about this from young to old knew that the big families were untouchable. Honestly, even just working at one of these companies is seen as a big deal in Korea, because it is understood that there are many benefits besides compensation when you are working for these companies. 

As an example, I had a friend in Korea who worked at Samsung, just a mid level position, but soon after joining the company he became close friends with the head of police in the town we were both living in, and whenever there was an issue with the law he would call his friend and then magically the problem would go away. This is just a small town example, so I can only imagine what the top guys are up to on a daily basis.


Edit for the people asking: During my time in Korea, I worked at 2 different Hagwons. The first was in a small town (of about 100,000, by Korean standards that is small) that I highly doubt anyone here would know by name, most Koreans  I talk to about it don't know about it. The second was at a major Hagwon in Seoul in the rich part of town, called Gangnam. I don't want to give the name because many celebrities' kids go to the school, but all you need to know is I met a lot of extremely rich people there. Like, several of my students' parents were CEOs, judges, politicians, etc.

Edit 2 for the people asking: I became friends with this Samsung employee because his younger brother was one of my students. At first, we would just chat in the lobby waiting for his brother. But over time we started hanging out outside of the school. Mostly because he wanted a foreigner friend to practice his English with, since he started going overseas often because of his new role at Samsung. Again, I am not 100% sure what his role was, we would just chat while drinking soju or eating food sometimes after work. That's all.

So for the people who are asking questions regarding his role, I genuinely don't know. And for people who think that is strange, I just want to say, I'm a guy, and like most guys I very rarely talk to my guy friends about their jobs. There are guy friends I have had for more then 10 years that I still do not 100% know what they do for work. All I know is that he told me he was in a "mid-level" position and that he was in charge of his own team. That's literally all I know, that and I believe he was in some aspect of promotion because I know he would go to different type of events around the world and around Korean fairly often. One time he got me into F1 for free when it was in Seoul because he had a booth there, and I was able to go behind the scenes. But that is literally all I know.

text:
South Korean media in general provides such a clear window into their ailing society. Kdramas almost ubiquitously touch on the themes of abuse of power, class based segregation, wealth disparity, and corruption. These shows are very often filled with entire casts of characters that both can't and won't strike back at the Chaebol's because of social and economic pressures. Despite this they also often feature these "good guy" Chaebol characters, usually sons and daughters, that I can't help but feel are forced in by executives that likely belong to these same upper classes to gaslight people into being less angry about everything.

Then we have the blossoming Korean Manhwa scene. This genre is filled to the brim with stories of individuals who were abused and mistreated in life, most often by their employers and the wider social constructs, who are then given a second chance at life with both their previous memories and some super-power which gives them an edge. A lot of these are revenge stories.

I imagine their literature and folk music isn't all that different.

It's honestly shocking how obvious the abuse faced by the Korean people is, and how little anyone cares to do anything about it.

I lived in South Korea for 4 months. Everyone has Samsung phones. But at least to me, most notably, you see Lotte Corporation everywhere from apartments (Lotte Castle), cinemas, fast food (Lotteria), liquor stores, malls, hotels, amusement parks, mascots, chocolate, towels, napkins, you name it, they probably have a hand in it. And it’s not just here and there. It’s in every corner. And that’s just the stuff you see. They also own various chemical companies, baseball teams, and other companies.

A few conglomerates basically own the country (like Lotte and Samsung), but it’s normal to them. The U.S. is heading there, if it’s not there already.

text: Using the ferry incident from 2014 in the intro is a very thin link to use as a segue into the main topic of the video of Chaebols as most of the public outrage was about many bigger factors that shouldn't have been glossed over. The protest videos you used were not because there were more containers on  the ship than regulation dictated, it was because of the terrible decisions the political leaders were making as the ship was sinking. Whilst it was still sinking, and as no coast guard was being dispatched to save the people, the president made an address saying everyone had been rescued. Parents waited on the piers for their children to come from rescue boats but no one came. There were also American navy ships nearby who offered to help but were explicitly told not to approach by SK. The only people to rescue the ones jumping from the ship were fishermen who happened to be nearby. Survivors recount that when they managed to get outside of the ship there was no one to help them. The public outrage was because of how the sinking was handled by the president and not because of ignoring regulations and things related to the Chaebols which came to light much later.

text: An oligarchy is a system enforced by the use of law to relieve an entity of the pressure of capitalism and its market, such as injecting a company with public tax or penalizing its competition via centralized economic planning, thereby creating a controlling class facilitated not by capitalism but by the government. It is essentially socialism just without a pretense of public good, but a pretense of capitalism. It is thusly definitionally anti-capitalist as it opposes and abolishes its principles in its operation. No such thing as capitalist oligarchy. Both Koreas suffer from a lack of capitalism, except one is terminal. Capitalism may be upkept only if economic regulations do not benefit individuals or entities by excluding or lessening the effects of free trade and the market. This is rare because government always seeks to increase its power and establish its control class. Even the company cartels in history were facilitated by corrupt governments, never the free market or supply and demand.

You’re the first and only reasonable comment I’ve seen on this kind of YouTube video. Thank goodness for that.

We South Koreans are very much in the same boat as Taiwan. If TSMC were to collapse, would the US really protect them from China? Probably not. In fact, I’ve even heard that some US politicians have suggested destroying TSMC’s semiconductor facilities before China could take them over. Honestly, I can’t blame them for thinking that way. After all, we know the US isn’t some miracle savior—they’re just using Taiwan and South Korea as military proxies. Even so, that’s still far better than being a puppet state of China.

That said, our big tech companies are not in the best shape right now. SK Hynix still has 19% of its facilities in China, and Samsung has been falling further behind TSMC in the foundry business since the 1990s. The gap has only grown worse over time. I doubt most of these YouTube commenters even realize that Samsung’s CEO was sentenced to five years in prison—though he only served one year. When he was released, the first thing he ordered was fried chicken, the food he craved most while in prison.

Samsung isn’t some Cyberpunk-like corporation like Arasaka. I get the joke, but it’s really not funny anymore.

It's understandable that some Indian individuals may feel frustrated w encounter restrictions at nightclubs based on their nationality. However, it's important to recognize that these restrictions are not driven by discrimination or racism. Rather, they may stem from concerns about misbehavior, such as excessive attention towards women in the nightclub.

Nightclubs are businesses aiming to provide a service and make a profit. They value their customers, including those from India and Pakistan. Unfortunately, there may be instances where individuals, regardless of their nationality, engage in inappropriate or disrespectful behavior towards others, particularly towards women. Such behavior can create discomfort and negatively impact the atmosphere of the nightclub.

In these cases, nightclub owners may implement restrictions not out of racism or discrimination, but as a measure to maintain a safe and enjoyable environment for all patrons. It's important for everyone, regardless of nationality, to behave respectfully and considerately towards others, especially in social settings like nightclubs. By promoting a culture of respect and modesty, we can contribute to creating more inclusive and welcoming spaces for everyone.

@Valhalla-rd1lj  The British brought the Hindu religion under one banner, but they didn't create it. Hinduism wasn't built by the British or even by us Hindus. It emerged on Indian soil through the collective actions of Indians, so there's no single founder of Hinduism. Its roots can be traced back to the Indus Valley civilization, and what we practice today has evolved over thousands of years. The British consolidated various religious practices under one name, but that doesn't mean Hinduism is a folk religion. It has its own rules and important religious texts like the four Vedas.

As for the discovery of the greatest bronze-age civilization - Indus Valley civilization (3300 BCE to 1300 BCE) that lasted 2000 years in India and the great Mauryan empire around 300 BC (the wealthiest country in the world during that period), the British found the sites and scripts. However, finding something is not the same as creating it. We Indians were the architects of these civilizations, and the British simply unearthed and brought to light the rich history that had been obscured due to the invaders’ destruction of our old universities and temples.

Who isn’t conquered and ruled? Every country has been conquered once and ruled = that is called history. Even Korea was conquered by all its neighbors but couldn’t do in return. But if there’s is any one country in the last 7,000 years that has cultural continuation and civilization continuity, it is India and only India. All our invaders couldn’t change us, they couldn’t change our genetics, they couldn’t change our language, they couldn’t change our culture. Europeans conquered Africa, America, and Australia, and it changed massively, but India didn’t. Today, 90% of Indians can’t even speak English. And there are just 1 million anglo indians in a population of 1400 million. How do you call that being conquered over? The Mongols, who conquered Asia and affected their culture and genetics, couldn’t invade India and lost. Only the Turks successfully conquered India, and their third generation was Indian - since they came to India and married Indians, the kings were all Indians - we don’t speak a Turkic language like Anatolia does (who were also conquered by Turks). 

The fact that it took the British 200 years, hundreds of wars, and still couldn't fully control the whole of India at once makes the term "conquering" even more absurd. Even when the British controlled large portions of India, many large kingdoms maintained full autonomy and paid taxes. Did the Brits do the same in other places? No, because they knew India was unconquerable. You simply cannot conquer us.

All of this means that the entire history is filled with uncivilized central Asian nomadic barbarians who are incapable of creating a civilization of their own, keep invading the greatest civilization in the history of humanity that is India, and failing to conquer it. The problem is that back in the day, lets says 1965 the cost of goods, real estate and everything was a lot closer to the median salary. Living was very very affordable back then on an okay job, 40 hours a week. Not only could you pay bills like that, but you could also make a whole lot more and save towards a property and a car very easily. Again, cost of goods and salaries were much closer to each other. Today in 2025, it's not the same. Inflation has continued, but the "GAP" between the cost of goods and salaries has simultaneously widened. The problem with our economic model is that it would require for salaries to also rise according to inflation. Even then, some assets have appreciated way too much and moved even well above inflation. Real estate increased by a factor of 21x in the last 60 years. The US dollar inflated by about 920% over the last 60 years. Home prices in 1965 median: 20k. Home price median today: 420k. Median salary in 1965 was 6,900, today in 2025 it's 61k. So salaries went somewhat along with inflation. Except, the buying power got fucked because the most important goods did not go along with inflation but crept way above it. Homes are just one example, but they are a massively important one. If it were to have gone along with inflation the median home price should be 200k, not 420k. It's more than twice of what it should be. That technically means that the dollar should be worth even less, considering you're basically paying double for a home that should be half the price it actually is. So despite statistics saying that 50k in 1965 is equivalent to 500k today, so 1000% increase, and salaries went from 6k to 60k...that's not true technically, when something like homes have 20xed in value over that same time frame. Technically means the dollar is worth a lot less than what economists say it is. The buying power argument might go for insurance or groceries, but certainly not homes, healthcare or even fuel. I sleep 4 hours a night tops, and have slept like that for many years. If I'm really lucky, I'll even get all four hours at once. Unfortunately, I don't get that lucky very often.

I am lucky in that I'm apparently wired to handle it well enough. If I'm going through an extreme bout of insomnia, things start getting real squirrely after a couple days of not sleeping at all. But it's more that I lose my temper more easily, and even start to momentarily lose balance and strict bodily control after ~55 hours of not sleeping. After 60+ hours of not sleeping, I'll occasionally go through micro dreams despite my eyes being wide open. For better or worse I've learned to deal with those well enough, and that's the point where I'll start taking meds to help put me under.

All that to say that sleep is far more important and more restorative than most people realize. It isn't until you chronically have to do without that you really start noticing all the real benefits of sleep that no one really seems to talk about.

This channel, and this video in particular, combed through other pieces -- starting with namely the extremely popular Kurzgesagt channel's piece on South Koreas declining birth rate, and then our OWN, dealing with the suicide rate, with Sulli as the specific celebrity example, with plastic surgery, and the thesis, the controversial accusation of American influence leading to pathological, cultural narcissism. He used specific stories, a narrative access point with the suicide bridge, and dove deeper, lingering on different focuses to wash it with his team, but it was plagiarism, pure and simple. If this upset you, I doubt you would enjoy our piece and analysis more, but we believed what we said in both of ours dealing with this subject, and we don't know what to do to watch it cobbled under what looks like an uncaring machine, under his apparatus, for the same cold capitalistic greed he claims Korea suffers from. 

We've tried reaching out, we tried posting, and when he could leave the comment up -- as we always do on our channel, no matter what -- and at least lie, and say he or his team never watched it, never found inspiration, -- it was instead deleted. 

Censored. 

We have kept the post.

We are a small channel. We are very, very poor. Single camera, no knowledge of production, and Jessica, my co-host, edits each piece herself, and she's no editor. We don't have the resources moon does. Like any channel, we want to grow or be mentioned when someone watches what we think we can offer, what we are proud of. 

I know this trick. I've plagiarized before. I know how to wash it with a specific story or, where the source mentions its thesis in passing, use a different source and then go deeper on the stat before alluding to the same one. 

In fairness, we were not the ONLY channel, the only piece, that sparked the light bulb for moons team to scramble and produce this piece, suddenly, like this, NOW. But kurzgesagt has no problem being a springboard for a content mills hungry machine. We do. It is because they are larger than even this channel. We are not. 

I dont know why I'm hiding this post here. I suppose I’m hoping it won't be deleted. I also suppose if you hated this one, then you would hate our OWN pieces for the wild claim we make as to the true systemic, generational pathology-of-a-disease killing this country slowly. I will seek out a few other comments to tuck this under, to cut-and-paste and hide it lest it get deleted, too.

I think it was the use of "narcissism," and an initial poster picking up on it. 

Anyway. Regardless. I'm fine with even one person knowing as we figure out what to do besides "feel slightly proud but also helpless and powerless and angry." It could help me sleep cleaner tonight simply knowing that I TRIED, and probably just yelled at clouds.

text: My grandfather was stationed in Japan and my mother was born on the US Air Force base in Tachikawa.  The atmosphere you are describing is fundamentally Japanese, but it's not necessarily because they are super friendly.  They are a society very geared toward service.  They smile and nod and sacrifice as a matter of duty.  They are very reserved and modest compared to western cultures.  For insurance, a feature on some toilets in Japan is the option to play music to cover any sound that may be overheard by others nearby.  They are restrained and some of the things we admire about Japanese culture, such as grace, comes from an extreme focus on carefully controlling movements.  Of course this is not an exhaustive dissertation, but hopefully enough to point out that what appears to be one thing to our eyes is actually quite another.  In other words, that polite smile and eagerness to be of service to you might just be the facade of a very unhappy individual.  There are a lot of pressures on both the Japanese and Koreans that lead to heartbreaking decisions.

I dont know why I'm hiding this post here. I suppose I’m hoping it won't be deleted. I have ADHD, and it has held me back all my life.  Not a day goes by without some aspect of it interfering with my life - usually because I forget things.  I have often wished that if I have to have some disability, I wish it was something physical so that people could see and understand it - but it's not like that.  I speak intelligently, and I am interested in many scientific subjects.  I spent my life in computer maintenance - though I was never a truly great employee.
My heart goes out to anybody with a disability similar to mine in a society like N. Korea.  People like me simply can't compete on a mental level.  Genetic disorders are physical in nature - that's why identical twins are identical - no genetic differences, so no physical differences - so ADHD, being a genetically inherited disorder, is a *_physical_* disability - but as it affects people mentally, that physical difference is in the brain - and I have recently learned that it can be seen on an MRI scan of the brain.  We all learn, as we grow through childhood, to use our brains differently - like being given a complex toy and figuring out what we can do with it - so the effects of ADHD are different in different people.  But my point is that people are all different - some are bright, and some are held back by one thing or another.  How do they manage in a country where shame is heaped on people who just can't compete?  It must surely produce a huge number of psychologically damaged people who consider themselves worthless.  Thank God my parents did not shame me for my inability to succeed, but encouraged me all the way, and I made a reasonably successful life

text:
Recent content farm-style critiques of South Korea’s social issues like this channel, and their subsequent memification, have struck a nerve with many Koreans, not necessarily because they deny the existence of problems, but because of how these problems are framed and presented.

Too often, these portrayals reduce complex societal issues to simplistic cultural explanations, or worse, imply that they are innate to Korean society or ethnicity. This kind of essentialist narrative ignores the far more important, structural factor: economics.

South Korea's economic activity is overwhelmingly concentrated in Seoul. For young people, they have little choice but to move to the capital. It’s an economic necessity. Obviously, this breeds intense competition in education, difficulty securing stable employment, and high housing costs — the top three factors that most directly affect whether young couples feel they can start a family.

These aren’t uniquely “Korean” problems, nor are they timeless cultural traits. They are modern, structural challenges exacerbated by urban overcentralization and decades of inadequate political response. Yes, there are other problems, like cosmetic surgery and K-pop(?). But these are superficial issues at best. To Koreans, it feels like an exaggeration to say that cosmetic surgery — or K-pop, K-drama, the suicide rate or what have you — explains, or even reflects, current social problems in Korea. Like gun violence in America, though, it's an issue easy to ridicule and make a meme out of.

text:
Great video. I am an American that lived in Greater Seoul area for 3 years back in 2002-2005 the early early days of the rise if K-Pop. I loved it so much, Korea, not K-Pop haha!!! , but interesting thoughts in this video are very similar thoughts I had back then towards ROK. Never was able to live in Japan. But I remember volunteering at local High School, doing conversation English.  Just show up and talk English and answer questions, play games.  I went once every 4-6 weeks. But even back then when I was lost I would look for a group students in uniform, walk over and say hi.  They would all be shocked and all giggle.  So I would wait for the giggle to pass, ask my question.  Then the group would hudle up like in American football, then assign 1 person to speak.  So I would get directions, restaurant reviews, everything.  Remember this was way way before any Translation App. 
I would take a few minutes, but worked everytime.  I went so much because my friends were all teachers and I worked for a big company nothing to do with teaching, but the kids in my area all started talking to me outside of school.  It was great in my little neighborhood.  So kids back then were really being pushed to learn English.  The Drinking encouragement was there back then, luckily I was in my late 20's so I could handle it, now in my early mid 50's I definitely could not hang anymore.
I loved Korea so much, even after 25 years if I could find a job there with my company I would take it.  I have even considered moving there in several years after I retire.

text:
I'll preface by saying this is simply my personal experience. I lived in both places - Japan first, then Korea. 2 Years more in Japan than in Korea. As a non-Asian, I liked Korea more. For me, I found Japan to have a facade that was hard to break, even after I learned a decent amount of Japanese. The people are polite, nice, and friendly in both countries. Both countries are clean, safe and easy to get around. And both countries have amazing sights and food. 

But Korea just has this... upfront honesty that doesn't make you feel as if you're doing something wrong or walking on eggshells. Japan, even within the major cities has this.... "we're us and you'll never be truly accepted" kind of attitude. Yes, that is something to be expected as a foreigner in any country but Koreans embraced me as a true member of their community, and has a direct politeness that's simply refreshing. 

It has been a few years, I've moved back home around 2018. But, I miss both countries, and Korea especially. Good to see its people, culture, and nation as a whole getting way more exposure these years. Cheers!

text: Lots of people saying Korea is for extroverts, but I am an introvert and I prefer Korea. I have lived 10years in Korea and 10 years in Japan. I am of Korean and Japanese ancestry (US citizenship) and speak both languages fluently. Yes, I like to be left alone, but in Japan, it was unbearably isolating to do that. I was forced to become somewhat extroverted in Japan so that I wouldn't go crazy. In Korea, people bother you enough so that you are able to decline and be like, "nah, I'll stay home tonight" but always have someone checking up on you so you're not isolated. I also prefer Korean food (Japanese food was very heavy/greasy and the healthier/traditional options basically all had the same taste and the vegetable options were very minimal when eating out.) There are lots more options for entertainment and ways to have fun without breaking the bank in Korea. In Japan, anything you did was extremely expensive. Costs overall are cheaper in Korea and you can find ways to cut costs. Also, I found Japanese to be in general nationalistic and although subtle, 99% of the people blatantly "othered" non-Japanese people. It didn't matter if my father was Japanese, I was "foreign" and thus not one of them. Every time I met a new person in Japan, they would say things like, "I bet you eat bread and potatoes everyday" "Can you use chopsticks?" etc. It was annoying to be stereotyped as if I were a white person from Kansas. I have always felt "accepted" by Koreans. They are curious about my birthplace, but they treat me like a distant cousin, which was refreshing.

I know many Americans who lived in Japan and Korea.  Big difference is that none of them have Japanese friends.  I mean true friends, not just acquaintances.  But they have Korean friends they keep in touch with.  Japanese are polite on the outside but very difficult to get close to.  Koreans are very direct but open.

EDIT: I see a lot of replies saying this isn't their case.  Of course there always are exceptions.  But in 'general', it is true Japanese as a young age are taught not to express their feelings.  There's even a term for it.  Honne and tatemae.  If you get past that, then yes, you can make Japanese friends.  But getting past that in the first place is what makes it more difficult than other cultures.
Also depends on your preference.  If you prefer people being nice to you on the outside and don't care what they really think, you'd love Japan.

text:
Having lived in Korea for many years and visited Japan several times, I agree with most of what was said in the video. But a few things the American woman in the blue shirt said left me scratching my head.

1. "Tokyo is a much bigger city than Seoul." 

Kinda? The metro area of Tokyo is bigger--37 million versus 25 million--but the central city areas are almost the exact same size. The special wards of Tokyo are 617 sq km with 9.7 million people. Seoul City is 605 sq km with 9.8 million. So Seoul is actually a bit more populous and crowded in terms of the actual city areas. 

2. "Japan is more American friendly." 

Japan and the US were enemies in WWII. In contrast, the Koreans viewed America as their savior. Obviously, that was decades ago, but it has colored the relationship between Japan and the US versus Korea. To wit, I hardly saw any American food places in Tokyo aside from McDonald's and the like. Tons of American food places are in Seoul these days. Plus, having US Army bases in and around Seoul means there is plenty of direct American influence in the city.

3. "Japan is more English friendly." 

The last time I went to Tokyo, some people could speak English, some signage was in English, etc. But pretty much every Korean under 30 speaks a decent amount of English and everywhere has English signs and menus aside from really old Korean restaurants. And Koreans have much higher scores on international English tests such as the TOEFL. Korea is actually among the top 5 English-speaking countries in Asia now. Japan is in the middle of the pack at best.

Yeah, some of her conclusions don't really match reality. But I can't deny that Tokyo is a great city, English-friendly or not, and if she feels more comfortable there, then good for her.

text:
For many foreigners, if they want to build deeper, non-superficial relationships, South Korea might be more suitable than Japan. This is because Koreans tend to express their thoughts and emotions more directly than Japanese people. Such a style of communication is closer to what many foreigners are accustomed to, making it easier for them to understand.

But what exactly does it mean to be a true friend? For some, it may mean openly sharing thoughts and quickly aligning values with one another. For others, it could be about maintaining a certain distance while gradually building trust through subtle interactions. It is understandable that many foreigners feel confused by Japan’s unique way of forming relationships, as it differs from their own customs.

Many Japanese people may feel disappointed when they hear foreigners say, “It’s difficult to build deep relationships with Japanese people.” Some might argue that Japan needs to be more open.

However, I don’t think that’s the case. People should interact with those they can truly understand, rather than expecting one side to change—whether that means “Japanese people should understand foreigners” or “foreigners should understand Japan.”

In conclusion, if someone holds an unrealistic fantasy about Japan based on anime or manga without truly understanding the reality, then coming to Japan will only bring disappointment to both that person and Japan itself.

text:
Lived in Korea for a year and visited Japan many times and worked there for a short time.
- Koreans are on average slightly better at English, apart from elderly people, who mostly speak little to no English.
- Most Koreans have traveled abroad a lot, while many/most Japanese people have just traveled within Japan.
- Both countries are very capitalist, but Korea is much more 'Americanized' than Japan.
- The work environment is insane in both countries, and overtime is the norm, but it is even worse in Korea, where even the government proposed increasing the work week to 69 hours.
- The salary used to be much higher in Japan than Korea, but today, they are about the same, while most things are still cheaper in Korea.
- The nature and countryside is beautiful in both countries, but there is 0 trash in Japan, and the infrastructure and buildings are better maintained in the countryside of Japan, and generally, the countryside of Korea seems to be a bit poorer.
- It is my impression that Koreans on average live a more fast-paced and insanely high competition "work hard, play/party hard" lifestyle, while Japanese people live a more down-to-earth lifestyle, where they do their best at fulfilling their duties to their boss, their family, and society, while valuing conservatism and perfectionism. I remember talking with a Korean guy, who moved to Japan, who told me that work and life was much more relaxing in Japan.
- In both countries, people are very respectful towards other people and towards the rules, norms, laws, and the order of society. I like to observe traffic and how people behave in transit, since I think that this to some degree reveals how people think and act in society. Traffic in Japan is extremely calm, orderly, polite, and quiet. I still have never experienced anything like the surreal experience of walking in Tokyo during rush hour with a million people walking past each other in this extremely organized way, without any noise at all. Korea is much more busy and fast-paced and even public busses in Korea drive fast and almost aggressively to make sure that they arrive as fast as possible. 
- The people from both countries are super nice. Koreans are more extroverted on average. However, people keep saying that Japanese people are cold, but I have never felt this way at all, and perhaps this is because I am from Denmark, where people are also known for being reserved.
- People in both countries are beautiful and know how to dress well. However, in Korea, people care extremely much about their appearance, and double-eyelid surgery is a common highschool graduation gift.
- I never felt the racism and hate towards foreigners that people keep mentioning. However, I have heard stories of racist and abusive employers in both countries, especially against people who don't look European.
- I love both countries, and I'm looking forward to visiting both again later this year!

text: My wife and I (both American) lived in Japan (Saitama & Gunma) ~25 years ago and Korea (Yongsan-gu, Seoul) ~20 years ago, and I found it interesting that not much has changed in terms of differences and the challenges to living in either country. Korea has changed a lot during this timeframe, so I expected impressions of foreigners living there to be different. We both miss living in both countries, and I have the privilege to visit both every couple of years for my job. I strongly prefer living in Japan & Korea than visiting. Maybe sometime in the future?

text:
Americans are generally more drawn to Japan than Korea for several reasons. Japan’s cities, such as Tokyo and Osaka, feature Western-style shopping malls, highways, and theme parks like Disneyland and Universal Studios, making Americans feel more at home. While Korea is modern and heavily influenced by Western trends, it maintains a distinct Korean urban aesthetic.

Japan also offers familiar global brands like Starbucks, McDonald's, and Apple, seamlessly integrating them into its unique cultural environment. While Korea has these brands as well, Japan’s long-standing embrace of Western goods feels more deeply ingrained in daily life.

Furthermore, Japan skillfully blends traditional elements with Western influences, particularly in its fusion of Japanese and Western dining and architecture. While Korea quickly adopts Western trends, it doesn’t blend them as harmoniously with its traditions as Japan does.

text: Honestly, I think Ms. Anna's experience is going to be a bit different than ours as foreigners, because, even though she lived abroad and can see how things are different, she is still Korean born and Korean by ethnicity.  We are very obviously neither ethnically or nationally Korean, and in places where everyone generally looks the same, people tend to be very curious about obviously different people.  I got addressed for conversation by a lot of strangers who wanted to practice their English, several middle aged+ women wanted to touch my naturally blonde hair, I had people stare into my eyes because they're naturally blue, I got catcalled, one of my female classmates poked my boob and asked if it was real, etc.  I think, in a lot of ways, the fact that I'm foreign and likely have different customs led to both them and myself using the "foreigner card" to excuse things that aren't typical Korean behavior, and in the same vein, natural curiosity often overrides propriety.  In no way was I offended, hurt or in any other way bothered by this, but that doesn't change that it happened.

text:
One thing that caught me by surprised was actually the cult recruiting! A couple of years ago (pre-pandemic), I went to Korea with my friend and we were just walking around the streets of Gangnam when a group of young adults came up to us and greeted us nicely. They told us that they were having a "cultural experience" at a nearby "tuition centre" and wanted us to join. Me being the very curious and naive student at the time, decided to tag along. We followed them to a slightly older building and went up the lift. By this time my friend and I were slightly hesitant and worried. Then we were brought into a room to have like a small "introduction" session with some other people. Afterwards they brought us to a different room and there was this prayer/offering shrine inside the room and they wanted us to pray there. At that point we just immediately ran out, took our shoes and even went into the lift barefooted. Went straight out and immediately took the train and left the area. While on the ride back we decided to google some more information as to what that whole experience was and at first I thought it was just some sort of scam but after a few more searches, it really was an actual cult recruitment. 

It really was a big lesson to learn that day and I hope other people traveling to Korea would be wary of that too. Apart from that incident, I had a really great time in the country!

text:
Totally agree as a Korean and she is talking about even some good things that many other youtubers don’t do.
Let me leave some more advices.
1. In the airport, do not accept the ride of taxi drivers that aren’t the airport one. They’ll charge you lots of fare much more than it has to be and you’ll end up  starting the first day in Korea as a nightmare. When you want to use a taxi, find the airport taxi service.
2. It’s not a good idea to ask for vegetarian menu in normal restaurants for locals. It’s true that many Korean foods come with vegetables but they are often mixed with meat-based sauce or something like that. If you are sensitive to your meal, Indian restaurants could be a good choice. I’ve heard that there are some vegetarian restaurants, but most of them are not so affordable.
3. Don’t smoke while walking and never do it when you’re with babies or children. It’s often considered as rude and uneducated one. 
4. Not a good idea to show your gender identity unless you’re asked first. As some other comments mention, Korea is more conservative than America, Europe and even some southeastern Asian countries are. Maybe young people will understand but Never do that to old people if you don’t want them to misunderstand you.

text:
Anna, if you allow me, I want to add my 2 cents to this discussion.
I have been living in Japan for more than 7 years, and part of the charm of being a Western foreigner in Asia is to break some of those social rules.
Sure, being respectful and not doing stupid things should be common sense (not saying to people to just break all rules and act like an idiot), but acting as a local will only remove the most important experience you could provide to all people around you. 
Hug people that you already know is a highly valuable experience for them (and in my personal experience, not a problem at all), dressing in different kinds of clothes can give them a different perspective of how things are outside their own country, etc... It is important to bring the "spicy sauce" of your cultural background to people's life. But (and this is a big BUT) be open to accept and enjoy the huge differences you will find.
And about the shoes, traffic lights, too much noise in public transportation, and approaching girls in the street, I totally agree... those are best practices whatever you are, just learn it and do, no matter which country you are!
In business, if it is your first time in Asia, people will laugh if you make mistakes like the business card. But, if you live here or have business often in this region, people will expect a little more. If you want to make a good impact, you should learn the basics and, if possible, the language (if not at a business level, at least, for a daily conversation). The basics include understanding your position in the conversation, how to treat people in different hierarchies, what they expect from you in your position, etc...

text: Many Indians romanticize Korean education and culture without understanding its dark reality. The term “SKY” (Seoul, Korea, Yonsei) isn’t just prestige — it represents an extremely toxic academic system, perfectly portrayed in a korean drama named "Sky Castle", where children are pressured, controlled, and mentally broken just to enter elite universities. Korea itself openly debates the damage this obsession causes, including depression and youth suicides, yet we selectively admire the aesthetic results without questioning the cost. Instead of blindly idealizing Korea, Indians should learn from its criticism — success achieved through fear, pressure, and lost childhoods is not something to glorify.

text:
I love watching Korean and Chinese dramas, but there are certain things that always bother me. One major issue is how employees are treated in workplaces. Overtime is shown as something almost mandatory, and employees, especially female employees are often treated badly. In many dramas, women are forced to go drinking with older CEOs, which I find really disgusting.
Another thing that shocks me is the bullying culture shown in these dramas. Pretty girls are bullied because others think they are “ugly,” and bullying is openly portrayed in high school dramas. At first, when I started watching K-dramas, I thought maybe it was just limited to a few shows where kids were unusually mean. But after watching many dramas, I realized that this behavior is shown as something normal in Korea.
They often bully people who are poor, those who don’t meet beauty standards, or children who don’t have parents. Honestly, this was very shocking for me. In our country, people who are poor or without parents usually receive extra kindness and support because others feel sympathy for them.
Now, I mostly watch these dramas only for their good storylines, and I’m no longer obsessed with them.
Another thing that bothers me is how they promote relationships before marriage. At first, things like holding hands or even kissing felt acceptable, but now they go to extremes as if it’s completely normal. What confuses me is that these dramas show society disliking women who get pregnant before marriage, yet at the same time, they portray innocent heroines going very far in relationships before marriage and no one seems to question it as long as she doesn’t get pregnant. They are even normalizing one-night stands. In some dramas, the hero sleeps with the heroine on the first night, she gets pregnant, disappears, and then suddenly returns years later with a grown child. After that, they fall in love again using the child as an excuse. Seriously???
And somehow, both the hero and heroine are still portrayed as innocent, pure, and extremely loyal. WOW.

text:
I live in Korea, did my masters here and focused on gendered crimes for the past 7 years of my studies. I've also worked in a government institute here as an intern focusing of criminology. I wanna shed some light on the living situation here as well, in the POV of a woman. 

All in all, it really isn't as safe for women as what many foreigners think. I've been stalked multiple times; my ex trespassed into my house, etc.

That being said, 4B isn't well known over here at all. In fact, it's rather coined by far radical feminists that Korean women feel have made the already sexist connotations of women worse. A majority of women here still wanna date, and others don't really want to because of the crazy socioeconomical standards. 

When I mean radical feminists in Korea, I don't mean individuals who work hard to fight for women's rights. They are people who think that women can do no wrong, which obviously isn't true. To make things worse, current DV and stalking laws are inadequate, while female protection policies are all passed for rather ridiculous things. (eg. most countries have a special department to deal with female SA victims respectfully-- not saying that men can't be SAed, but statistics do show a huge difference. However, DV is heavily equalized and seen as a family issue. Stalking was only seemed a crime because no harm was done) 

Mostly, 4B movement did start in Korea, but it was only within a small group of women. We are all aware of the dangers in dating here so I ain't dating now, but it truly isn't that bad. There simply isn't enough time-- we're all overworked, inflation is crazy, the basic pay range for new graduates are between 2.5~3 grand USD. However, housing prices are estimated to sky rocket to 1.2 million USD ish in Seoul. 
I do agree that new policies have to made and I really see all the gendered problems in Korea as a MASSIVE issue. However, if 4B is made popular, it's probably going to make things worse. 


I wish all women stay safe and one day, education from young + strong repercussions can finally reduce the crazy number abusers.

​ @MiskoGe  RE: "state ownership is not collective ownership."

Great point!

You're absolutely right — in theory, socialism advocates collective ownership by the people. But in practice, especially in early 20th-century socialist states like the USSR, China, Cuba, and others, this was implemented as state ownership.

This shift happened largely due to the urgent need for rapid industrialization and modernization in largely agrarian societies. The state, governed by a centralized party, claimed to act as the collective representative of the people, managing nationalized enterprises, farms, and factories through centralized planning.

It’s true that Western critics often argued that, in practice, only a small political elite benefited, while workers remained disempowered — essentially replacing private capitalists with a bureaucratic class.

However, it’s also important to note that after the collapse of the Soviet Union, independent polls across countries like Russia, East Germany, Ukraine, Serbia, and Moldova consistently found that a majority of adults who had lived under Soviet-era socialism expressed a preference for it over the post-communist market capitalism that followed — particularly citing better economic security, social stability, and access to healthcare and education.

text:
I've watched videos of a few North Korean defectors who were extremely depressed while living in South Korea bc they were treated very poorly. They ended up moving to the US (these few ppl whose videos I watched) and they were much happier. We don't judge them or treat them poorly (according to them), we are the opposite: happy for them, eager to help, full of encouragement. We also don't have such stigmas surrounding mental health as we used to, or as many other countries currently have. They said they got enough education and government assistance to get them on their feet. I hope that's true for anyone who escapes North Korea to make their way to the United States, that we are the polar opposite of what the regime told them we were.

Edit: I'm not saying that South Korea is a bad place, of course. I just thought it was interesting and pretty spiffy that the ppl who came here with the assumption that Americans viscerally hated them (that's what the propaganda made them believe) were very pleasantly surprised to learn that most of us are not actually like that.
