text: Earlier this year I went to a college campus as a hs sophomore when, while I was minding my own business on a bench reading (unperformatively, mind), these students came by to chat w me bc they thought I looked cool. I was unnerved bc what were college students talking to me for?-until they told me that THEY were hs sophomores too, and they thought I was the college student. That confirmed a lot of things to me. I have to remind myself sometimes that I don’t get a latent period of patience when interacting with strangers bc they don’t realize I’m young. I was offered drugs and other things freely in Europe. It’s almost as though with how much the internet has promoted “put-together-ness” it’s evaporated young people’s moment in their lives where how they developed on the inside was meant to match their development outside. It’s weird having to play catchup with my own personality and mental development. It’s weird that while in America they promote individualism, we all share a collective vanity. Or rather it functions as vanity, but it’s in service of achieving societal acceptance. It’s an anxiety. It relieves us of the blame if I were to say we were “forced to grow up”, but there’s little other phrasing to use.

I distinctly remember the first time I felt ugly, and it was when I had first started listening to Kpop. It was 2009, I was age 11/12, and I got really into Girls Generation. I remember watching their music videos on Youtube and thinking about how beautiful they were, and looking at myself in the mirror and realizing I did not look like them and therefore I must be ugly. I spent a significant amount of time during my teenage years thinking about plastic surgery, despite knowing that I didn't really want it. I just wanted to feel beautiful. I am still working on unpacking that and I'm now almost 28.

All that happened prior to Instagram and TikTok, I truly cannot imagine growing up as a teenager right now, with all the blatant marketing designed to make you feel ugly. Of course this kind of marketing is nothing new, but when before you would only see it on tv or magazines, now it follows you around in your pocket.

What's wild to me is how easily dysmorphia can set in even w/people w/really secure self image. After covid I started getting lash extensions (by comparison to plastic surgery a super harmless enhancement). 

At first they were really conservative wispy barely there - a year in I had super unflattering volume lashes and couldn't see that I was overpaying to look actively bad. I also started developing a sensitivity to the glue and kept going 5-6 sessions later. My aesthetician also didn't stop me from getting a more extreme look. It took almost a year to adjust to myself without them but now that I have I think I look much better with the subtly of my own lashes. 

People w/plastic surgery can never go back to their original features for that comparison. That mild experience has put me off from more permanent work forever because for a full year I truly felt strange and less attractive in my own skin when the opposite was true. 

I can't imagine trusting a clinic who has never met you and also may not share your aesthetic values to bring out the best in your features AND tell you no even if it's less profitable.

text:
I live in Korea and I cannot stress my issue with the plastic surgery industry here is predatory. People will go on and on about how it's a choice people make, and we should honor this choice. While I'll never hate or go after someone getting work done, I think it's so disingenuous to not acknowledge that majority of EA [but very heavily in Korea] will groom and prey on the people into getting work done. I will never not talk about the way that photoshopping ID cards [in front of you too and without asking] and the looming ever-present way filters are pushed here and companies are fined for handing out plastic surgery fliers to children outside of their school, continue to trick young audiences that you will not survive without work being done and hating how you look.

Also the photo thing isn't completely gone from my experience. I was still required to provide a photo for my interviews 3 years ago, and because of in person interviews you will still often be judged based on your appearance/clothing when you go in to meet with potential jobs. I'd also personally argue this whole "Korea doesn't shame people for getting work done" is still a structural lie, for most you need to have work done but not know you have work done. If you have too much people will still be very catty to the average person, while the main people 'exempt' from the judging tend to all be those with fame. Korean society will still shame you, and still will hate you if you have work done to some level all while telling you that you still need it/need more.

text:
I'm torn in two drastically different ways on this issue. For one thing, I've had palpable dysmorphia since I was 11 years old. It was the beginning of the baddie era and I had to hear all about being fat with no butt, how my budding boobs didn't count because I was fat, so on and so forth. Lookism and desirability as social capital are thoughts that have ruled my life for the past 12 years since my dysmorphia took root. I have a list of invasive and non-invasive procedures I'd start getting done in a heartbeat if I could, and the list has only grown over the years...

...on the other hand, this stuff makes me SO 👏🏻 RAGEFUL 👏🏻 AND 👏🏻 SAD. Being objectively ugly breaks you out of the Matrix early in life tbh, you learn patterns of behaviour in people and how to compensate for what you don't have in social capital to get by. It messes me up to see how image-conscious, insecure and straight-up dysmorphic Gen Z is as a generation, especially when it's all BULL. Facial harmony is just repackaged phrenology; skinny is desirable because it was a Victorian beauty standard that started with goddamn TUBERCULOSIS. THE FETISHISM OF THINNESS IS LITERALLY THE FETISHISM OF ILLNESS. The BBL wave made me feel for my Black friends who grew up being bullied for having big bottoms and were now suddenly thrust into fetishism. The first rhinoplasty was done on a man who just felt that his nose was too big.

Guess what, you idiots? IT'S RACISM, CLASSISM, AND CAPITALISM ALLLL THE WAY DOWN, BABY!!!! And guess what again?! Plastic surgery is NEVER a personal choice, because you're a collectivist creature in a society. Every choice you make as it is is influenced by someone or something, and there's no way to excise the opinions and standards of society from the choice to get plastic surgery. It's okay to feel a way about yourself, it's okay to be curious about procedures and what they'd do to you, but my god standards are fickle and beauty fades and YOU ARE SO MUCH MORE THAN ALL OF IT!!!

I never became friends with someone because I thought they were hot. Of course, there's physical attraction in a crush, but I don't have a type and I enjoy so many different kinds of people. We are one of the most morphologically diverse animals on the goddamn planet bro, we need to actually embrace that for the cool and awesome happenstance that it is. 

TLDR; I hate myself so goddamn much, it sucks, it hurts, but I'll never fall for the grift of vanity procedures. You shouldn't, either. I bet you've got a cute nose and pretty lips. Would suck to see them go.

text: I stayed in Korea for a few weeks in 2019 and then a year from 2021-2022. Lookism, this societal pressure, is insane there compared to my home country (in Europe). I've heard Korean friends who lived abroad for a while and returned to Korea complain about it a lot too. In Seoul, it seemed like everyone below the age of 50 and many above it were styled from head to toe every day. Women AND men. Their outfits were cohesive and put together, hair was styled, I rarely saw women without makeup. At some cafés and stores it seemed as if all their (probably part timer) staff looked almost the same (and no, I am very good at differentiating Asian faces). One friend even told me that some places only hire people that fit a certain type. Big advertisement posters for surgery clinics are common at subway stations too, something that's heavily regulated and rarely ever seen in my home country. But there was also a palpable difference between Seoul and other smaller cities, even Busan seemed a lot more relaxed in terms of beauty standards.

text: ive done medical tourism before, but not for cosmetic surgery. i went for a chronic pain treatment because i wasnt able to get any care in my home province and wait lists were over a year long while i was housebound/bedbound. my parents used all their savings so we could travel to Italy to get a treatment there that is still in the process of getting approval in North America, but was studied well in Europe. we went through a medical tourism company because i only know enough Italian to order dinner, and we were all stretched thin at the time. it did work for a short time and gave me some quality of life back. as someone who’s benefited from medical tourism, i think it’s a great indicator of the flaws people are experiencing with their healthcare at home. i really don’t think the medical tourism industry should exist because people should be able to get skillful, timely, and accessible care at home, but for some people like me it’s a life saving industry.

text:
Mina this is such a great video! I’m often hesitant to watch videos of non-Korean people talk about Korea because of it being misrepresented or viewed in a very American-centric gaze, but this was so well researched and empathetic to what Korean women go through as well. (But also not letting Korea off the hook regarding its soft power and what it’s done to contribute to systemic oppressions of South Asians as well)
I’m Korean American but grew up in Korea until I was 18. I still remember my aunt walking me around plastic surgery clinics in Gangnam under the guise that she was going to get consultations, but they were all actually for me regarding getting double eyelid surgery. The self-policing that women (and men!) do here is so pervasive and deeply embedded in our culture. It’s hard to shake the feeling that everyone is low level judging the way you look and dress, and I don’t think I’ll ever be able to completely overcome the feeling that I don’t measure up to an “objective” beauty standard. It really affects my self image and how I navigate relationships even in the US now. 
Thankfully I think some things are changing, I’m a lot more comfortable walking around Korea now and I genuinely feel like people allow for some diversity in appearance, but we still punish women like those in the stop the corset movement who push too far against the grain.

text: As usual, thanks for another well researched and thoughtful video. As a senior, I remember the pressure to 'look good' but I also appreciate growing up in a culture of using non surgical means to bring out each individual's unique beauty. And underlying that was an understanding that inner qualities like intelligence, character, talent etc. were more important. I'm horrified by the K Pop pressure to make the stars all look alike. I feel lucky that my family had deep values and didn't consider popular culture to be very important. It happens that my expertise is film, but my favorite films are international films with stars that look like real people and deal with serious subjects, and are also uplifting on some level. Jean Renoir said the value of being a filmmaker was continuing to always learn more, be curious, care about the meaning of life etc.  I think you are lovely, Mina and very much a deep, intelligent individual. Thanks again for this video!

this is your first video that almost made me cry. I love learning about beatury/cinema history, I get angry with videos like the Shein trend or influencer trips... They're all amazingly well done.

Wrost part of all? I know that some people die after getting the precedure and "I don't care". It's sad how we teach girls and women that it's okay to risk your life if that means you have a chance to be pretty. 
I hate learning about the Korean beauty industry (but at the same time it fascinates me) because I check none of the characteristics to be considered pretty. I've always wanted to travel to different Asian countries, but I don't want people staring at me for being fat and masculine

I'm already considered ugly here in Spain, so I can't imagine how am I considered in places like Korea, Japan, China or Vietnam

In Malaysia, if a student mentions ISIS, it usually doesn’t refer to the extremist group.

Most likely, they mean the Institute of Strategic and International Studies (ISIS Malaysia) — a government-linked think tank that does research on economics, security, and policy. It often works with universities and hosts seminars, conferences, and internships for students.

If the context is news or security, then it could mean the militant group “Islamic State of Iraq and Syria.”

Comparison of Malaysia versus US
1. Weather: Malaysia is summer the whole year with 8 months of thermoneutral weather, where you do not need heating or cooling. US has 3 months. Malaysians consume 1/3 the eletricity of US citizens
2. Extreme Weather: Certain Malaysian states on east coast get flooded but only during monsoon season. US has hurricanes, floods, windstorms, storm surges, tornadoes, wildfires, cold waves and heatwaves, droughts, permafrost , winterstorms, tsunamis, earthquakes 
3. Cost of living: 76% lower than New York, 66% lower than Los Angeles, 72% lower than San Francisco, 63% lower than Chicago, 53% lower than Houston, 65% lower than Seattle,70% lower than Boston, 66% lower than Miami, 59% lower than Austin, 54% lower than Las Vegas, 67% lower than San Diego. If you live like a Malaysian family of four, it will cost you $1317 per month..in the most expensive city. Similarly if you are single cost of living if you live like a Malaysian will be $395 a month 
4. Fuel cost : Malaysia is the 9th lowest in the world which in turn affects eletricity, driving cost, transportation cost, flight tickets 
5. Internet: Malaysia is $0.28 pergigabyte. US is $6.00 per gigabyte. That is more than 20X. Talk about ripping you off. Internet speed is 105mbps versus US 127
6. Inflation: Malaysia had lower inflation 6 out of last 10 years
7. Property Purchase: Malaysians pay 38% of income for mortgage payments. US citizens pay 53%. If I were you, I would just sell my US property at average of $400K, come to Malaysia buy 4 properties, 1 to live in and rent out the other 3. Home ownership rate is 77% versus 66% in US. Your prices, interest rates and repayment rates are much higher

You're asking about what “ISIS” stands for in Malaysia—and it indeed stands for something very different from the extremist group.

In Malaysia, ISIS refers to the Institute of Strategic and International Studies Malaysia. This is a well-established, autonomous think-tank founded on 8 April 1983, focused on policy research in areas such as economics, foreign policy, security, nation-building, social policy, technology, innovation, and environmental studies .

It's important to note that despite sharing the same acronym as the militant group "Islamic State of Iraq and Syria," the two are completely unrelated. In fact, when concerns were raised about the similarity, a government minister reaffirmed that the institute would not change its name.

So, in short: ISIS Malaysia is not a militant organization—but a respected policy research institution.

text: I think the reason Kat works as a “not like other girls”  character without us hating her is she’s not actually “not like other girls” - she’s just not like the other popular girls in her school. She has a girl friend she likes so she doesn’t hate women in general. (Usually the “not like other girls” characters have a male best friend cause “girls are too much drama” lol) Her interests aren’t portrayed as “only she likes these things cause she’s so much more special than everyone else” because there’s plenty of other women at the concert she’s enjoying. And the biggest thing - She doesn’t use her “not like other girls”ness to get the attention of men or to undermine other girls. She doesn’t hate her sister for being pretty and popular, she just doesn’t like the attention due to her own trauma and has different interests because of that. It also helps that this was before the feminist characters had to be Mary Sues so her flaws actually make her more relatable and sometimes more likable as a character.

@williamg3427 Thank you for sharing your experience. I’m sorry to hear that your time in Korea felt uncomfortable.
I’d like to offer another perspective that might help explain what you experienced.
In Korea, people tend to avoid initiating conversations with strangers not because they dislike others, but because they worry about disturbing someone’s personal space or time. For many Koreans, not approaching first is actually considered a form of politeness.

This cultural norm can feel very different from places like Canada or Thailand, where greeting strangers is a natural sign of friendliness. I understand how the contrast might have felt cold or unwelcoming.
However, many Koreans show warmth and kindness once a connection is established, and they often try their best to be respectful in ways that may not be immediately visible. Cultural expectations of politeness can simply look different from country to country.

I genuinely hope that if you ever visit Korea again, you might encounter moments that show another side of the people here. Every place has a wide range of experiences, and I hope your next ones are better.
Wishing you safe and pleasant travels wherever you go next.

text: I get what you're saying. I recently watched another YouTuber who is hafu (half Japanese and, in this case half black). She said, even though she was born in Japan and lived there most of her life (she moved to the States with her parents and stayed for 4 years of highschool before moving back to Japan), she gets treated as a foreigner because of her appearance. To elaborate, despite her Japanese heritage and cultural roots, and even being a native Japanese speaker, she notices that she gets treated as a foreigner, which has its perks because she doesn't experience the same cultural and vocational pressures that her fully Japanese relatives and friends face. text: I feel the prison comparison is a false equivalency. People under the threat of death while under the guise of freedom experience fear and limitations with no end in sight, having done nothing wrong except be born in the wrong country. A person serving their sentence receives an opportunity to atone for something they did wrong, and if they do it well, they slowly regain freedoms until they are released. They do return to a world that requires them to learn new skills and a new way of life, but their lives after prison aren't in a wholly new environment. Being plucked from the only world you've ever known and moved into a new one, especially one with a new language and culture, is completely jarring. Criticism: Some economists and commentators argue that the ARP, passed under President Biden, contributed to inflation by injecting significant federal spending into an already recovering economy. Context: Supporters counter that it aided a rapid jobs recovery (16 million jobs created by 2023) and halved child poverty temporarily, but the inflation critique persists among detractors.
Affordable Care Act (ACA) - 2010 (Obamacare)
Criticism: Critics, including some healthcare professionals and Republicans, claim the ACA increased premiums for certain groups (e.g., middle-class individuals not qualifying for subsidies) and led to a loss of preferred doctors or plans due to mandated coverage requirements. Some argue it strained small businesses with compliance costs, potentially hindering job growth.
Context: Proponents highlight expanded coverage to 31 million previously uninsured Americans by 2023, but the policy’s complexity and cost shifts remain points of contention.
Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) - 2022
Criticism: Some analysts suggest the IRA’s climate and healthcare investments, while aimed at long-term benefits, added to federal spending (estimated $738 billion over a decade), potentially exacerbating the national debt (projected to hit $35 trillion by 2025). Critics on X have called it a corporate handout, questioning its effectiveness in curbing inflation, which remained above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target into 2025.
Context: Supporters point to its investments in clean energy and drug price caps, but fiscal conservatives highlight debt concerns.
Dodd-Frank Act - 2010 (Financial Regulation)
Criticism: Opponents argue this post-2008 financial crisis reform imposed excessive regulations on banks, stifling lending to small businesses and contributing to slower economic growth. Some claim it increased compliance costs, which were passed onto consumers, and didn’t prevent future banking issues (e.g., Silicon Valley Bank collapse in 2023).
Context: Defenders credit it with strengthening financial stability by curbing risky practices, though its long-term economic impact remains debated.
Expansion of Child Tax Credit (CTC) - 2021 (Temporary under ARP)
Criticism: While it reduced child poverty by nearly 50% in 2021, some critics argue its expiration in 2022 left families worse off, creating a "cliff effect" that increased financial instability. Others suggest it discouraged work among low-income parents, potentially impacting labor force participation.
Context: The policy’s short-term nature and lack of renewal have been points of regret among some Democrats, with mixed economic outcomes.

It's almost like reading my own diary from my 20s, I remember leaving Singapore to Canada at 22, thinking I would be back later, that my home would always be my home. Fast forward 4 continents and 76 countries, I am 43 now and nothing is waiting for me in Singapore anymore, my family is no longer there, the one I have left is the one I made. 
Home is not a place, to me it was my parents, and they've been gone for a few years now, so Singapore is just another city I visit with nostalgia, tearing me apart between extreme sadness and a smile, never in between. We settled in Luxembourg, kids are growing up nicely, I hope they realise sooner than I did that it's not about the colour of the grass, it's about stepping into the other side. I have a feeling your departure is somewhat related to that conclusion.
I wish you and your loved ones an adventurous 2025 :)

Everything must shine...and the dark side? We just try not to talk about it, we don't show it. I am mostly worried about the next generation, so different from their parents and grand parents who worked so hard for them, and understand the value of each penny. 

I hope things will change, but....

I'm writing as a 21-year-old Korean. Currently, Korea is grappling with a serious population crisis and a low happiness index.
Korea's societal values and standards for life and happiness are extremely limited and rigid. As a result, many Koreans feel unable to live their own lives. Instead, they become trapped in endless comparisons with others and live what is often referred to as a 'universal life.'

In this pursuit of a universal life, many Koreans sacrifice their individuality, live according to others' standards, and express hostility toward anything that deviates from what is considered universal.
Korea might be the most diverse country in the world when it comes to hate speech and swear words. The troubling part is that this hate isn't directed at those who violate social norms in harmful ways. Rather, it's aimed at anyone who dares to live differently or fails to meet what society deems a 'universal' standard of success.

This societal atmosphere has shifted Koreans' life goals away from intangible values like love, family, friendship, happiness, personal growth, and hope for the future. Instead, life has become a race to accumulate comparable material values like wealth, appearance, academic achievements, and prestigious careers.

Korea is sick.

Even more alarming is that no one in politics seems genuinely concerned about Korea's future.
In fact, this culture of comparison, hate, divide sides is a favorite tool of political leaders. Political parties exploit division for their own gains, focusing on taking sides and discrediting opponents rather than engaging in productive discussions or crafting meaningful policies.
I've been interested in politics since middle school, but looking at Korean politics often feels like watching a religious war—fanatical, divisive, and unproductive.

(Sighs)...
There’s so much more I want to say, but this comment is already too long, so I’ll try to summarize.
Korea is facing many urgent problems that need to be addressed. While I have criticized the political community, I also recognize that some of these issues are part of Korea’s growing pains.
The country’s rapid growth has brought remarkable advancements, but it has also led to significant side effects.
You can get a sense of Korea’s growth pace by watching this (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QYkcVbaXfPw). Perhaps, in these rapidly changing times, people feel lost and tend to stick to paths already paved by others because they are afraid to forge their own.

I hope Korea becomes a more mature and admirable country.

((The sentence might be a bit awkward, but I did my best😁))

text: Certainly, Korea has its 'dark' side, or rather "social problems." However, compared to homelessness, drug abuse, school shooting, school violence, poverty, high tuition fees, racism, etc. in many Western countries, Korea;s problems seem less serious.  My nieces and nephews back home cannot dream of buying a house /apartment, pretty much the same as here.  Plus, living in EU  and Canada and I'm pretty sure US, is much more expensive than here in Korea. I was in Europe and Canada last summer and the prices of most products and services shocked me. Plastic surgery and extreme dieting are normalized here, but still the majority of my students look normal and untouched, plus they are getting chubbier due to the change in diet. The reason I'm leaving this comment is to say it's really (still) not so bad. Also, I'd fact check the tour guide's claims. Korea is Seoulcentric but to say that there's nothing outside of Seoul is gravely exaggerated. Everywhere, there's good infrastructure and there are big cities like busan, Daegu, Incheon... There's a trend of people moving outside of Seoul and more and more choosing alternative lifestyles not just wanting a job with a corporation and a big house in Seoul.

text:
I liked your video but I think that anyone who is into k-culture is very aware of the not so good parts of South Korea. To be honest, I want to see all sides of a country that I visit, not just the good parts (that’s like only having a starter course of a 3 course menu).

I was in Seoul last week, someone here I’d wanted to visit for so long. I was worried that I’d built it up in my mind and it would fall short of my expectations. How wrong I was. It blew me away. I’ve been lucky enough to travel a lot and I’ve lived in different countries for work, but nowhere blew my mind like South Korea.

The main thing that I wasn’t expecting was how amazing the people are. I knew that they could be more reserved than westerners, but they were the kindest, friendliest people I’ve ever met. We had Halmonis giving us sweets and fruit, young people asking if we needed help if looked a bit lost trying to get a taxi ( use Uber if you are a foreigner, it works brilliantly in Seoul) to kindness on every level. People seen to actually be aware of their fellow humans instead of being completely self centred.

I know about the education system, the suicide rates and the insane pressure to keep up but this country only had its first fully democratic elections less than 40 years ago. It is culturally and politically very young, despite the way it looks. I’m hopeful that they will tackle the issues they are living with and in turn South Korea will mature into a happier place for people to live in.

text:
Hi! I'm a Korean and I live in a rural city. For 13 years I lived in Seoul. I think the guide June does not really know this country and the history. Korea, China, and Vietnam had been performing "Gua-geo jae," which is national examination for electing public officers for more than a thousand years. If a child passed this exam, the whole family got rich and safe. Therefore, parents really wanted their children to pass the exam; and this tradition and attitude became nowadays's educational culture. Koreans have studied very hard since 7th century. 
Although the guide said that there are no infrastructure and medical services in the rural areas, as living in the rural city, I am very satisfied with my life and my city. I can see professional doctors whenever I want; I can buy food and natural ingredient cheaper than in Seoul; housing prices are also cheaper than in Seoul.

Therefore, don't believe what the guide said. His words are partially true.

P.S. I learned English at Korean public schools between 1990s and 2000s. I really appreciate Korean public school system.

text:
I thought expectations on Japanese students were inhuman. Saturday used to be a full school day, and children were expected to be involved in extracurricular activities which could keep them at school until dusk. Weekends and holidays were taken up with sports competitions and school events. However, urban students or those that wished to enter high status schools (particularly university) also had to go to cram schools to study for entrance exams or to excel at school. Here, students learned things that were more advanced than their grade level. This lasted until well after dark.

While living in Japan, I learned that life for students in South Korea was even worse. Japanese celebrity panels watched in shock as South Korean students were shown studying at their cram schools, or even their regular schools, until 11 p.m. each day (as in maybe Sunday as well). They were provided space to sleep if necessary. It was considered normal. Also, as opposed to Japan which has a number of prestigious universities (though of course Tokyo University is at the top), South Korea at that time only had THREE national universities which students aspired to. In a nation of 70 million people. Imagine the level of competition.

The price of South Korea's success and expectations placed on the younger generation is coming back to haunt them. I was not aware that the situation outside urban areas was so dire. Japanese prefer large cities, but living in the countryside or small islands does not mean a lack of infrastructure or even hospitals. It's just much less convenient. People may need personal vehicles to go about their daily life. I've lived that life in Japan.

Then I learned of what Chinese students went through to enter prestigious universities which was the ultimate soul crushing thing I could imagine. Just imagine that the Chinese students we see overrepresented in America's most famous universities (18% in my son's Ivy) are the REJECTS of the Chinese system. A Chinese high school student is allegedly better educated (particularly in maths) than American university graduates. Chinese as on YouTube call American school a vacation, even as they excel by US standards. In a language foreign to them, I must add. Chinese students as I knew them while going to college in the late 1980s spoke Chinese amongst themselves, and took notes in Chinese. Yet they could still get perfect grades.

text: As a Korean, I wouldn't particularly recommend Myeongdong to foreigners. While it is undoubtedly the most famous area, I believe there are better places to spend your time that are more authentic, more representative of Seoul, and more traditional. Myeongdong, simply put, is more typical than traditional. It is a place where overpriced souvenirs that appear "Korean" but lack genuine roots are sold, and it is also very crowded. When foreigners visit Korea, I think the unique vibe of Korea is a significant factor (since we lack vast natural landscapes). Therefore, if one wants to experience Korea's indie culture, I would suggest Hongdae. For traditional culture, Gyeongju is ideal, where one can feel the coexistence of life and death through the numerous tombs scattered around daily streets and villages, as well as the Daereungwon Tomb Complex. Jeonju Hanok Village is another excellent choice for traditional experiences. Insadong in Seoul has traditional aspects, but its current appearance is far from traditional and is overly commercialized in a negative way, offering little value. For a lively seaside city experience, Busan is great, and while Jeju Island has everything, its downside is the extreme expense.

text:
My experience in Korea was similar to yours. I'm 30 something, I did a career change (software development) to teaching. I finished 2 contracts and then I went to Shanghai.

I really fell in love with the city. I'd get off work early and explore parks, trendy art areas, eat some amazing mango-jelly desserts, do book shops. Just a stellar place with a little bit of every part of the world in one metropolis. Especially for artists and creatives. I think nowhere tops it.

The teaching side of things can be precarious though so I felt compelled to leave a message here. 

Holidays have to be mostly made-up by working extra days on weekends. This left me dreading any kind of holiday because it usually meant working 6+ days straight. And this happens about every month. 

If you decide you dislike your job and you want to give your 30 days notice, expect the school or agency try to illegally withhold your salary from the last month or two. They might deny releasing you. They can try to spam immigration with fake work permit applications so you either stay with them or have to leave China. It's not legal, but time is not on your side so most people usually cave.

Imagine how much control an employer has over you once you're locked in a job.

In the classroom, you'll likely feel more relaxed. The kids sleep for 2 hours after lunch. They play. But I felt pointless. There was little to no teaching happening. You're supposed to be an entertainer who happens to speak English. We were asked to hide English books during inspections.

I struggled with work happiness but I loved my time in the city. I only lasted 6 months.

I do love helping people, making kids laugh, and being involved in positive community building but it was tough for me.

If you really want to go there to teach, there are ways to land 2-month paid vacation jobs in bigger campuses around Suzhou (30 minutes from Shanghai) and get paid well. The classroom experience might be better than what I had.

In my case, I definitely want to live in Asia again, I would prefer being some kind of digital nomad or working in a university and trying to settle down somewhere. Thank you for sharing your experience with us.

@asha-vahishta  
1. Yes! But I still do it in my free time. Trying to transition back by starting up my own ed-tech projects and other things. 

2. No, mostly because I stepped out for too long. It's actually quite hard to get a coding job again if your CV/resume includes big gaps where you were doing other things. I don't regret it but I do think it's something a person has to consider very carefully.

If you're just looking to experience life elsewhere but are happy to keep doing the same work, then definitely look for coding jobs in the target country.

3. Massively. I felt empty before, like I was wasting my time, waiting for retirement, and not doing anything very meaningful. I was becoming unhealthy, spiritually demoralized, etc. You can always make money, but time is gone forever. 

If you're really serious about going overseas, and not getting a regular office job again, I would recommend 2 options:  
-transitioning to university teaching
or
-starting your own business, preferably online

Take serious steps to invest in either of those two options and you're likely to find a happy, stable, well-paid career with good work-life-balance. You don't need a big salary, you just need to be in the right place with proportional conditions.

The future of employment is so up in the air right now, and anyone thinking they can just retire on doing whatever they're doing could be surprised in just a few years as companies downsize further or the value of work diminishes.

If you feel like you vibe with a particular country, (I was surprised how much I loved Shanghai), then just work towards it. Lots of people are trying to figure out ways to make their money go further.

If you search for 'all akiyas' you'll find examples of $30,000 to $60,000 houses in Japan that you can renovate, add solar, and work from home instead of putting out $500,000 for a house in the States. That's just one example of what expats do but there are more. Imagine buying a home for 50K, investing another 50K in starting your own business, etc.

I think the big salaries in the hyper-expensive economies can lead to an illusion of happiness.

It's possible in China to save 2,000 to 3,000 $ a month after all expenses with teaching k-12 school age kids, but there are many scams. In Korea, you can maybe save 1,000$. But honestly, the industry is collapsing so I don't recommend these jobs for a lot of the reasons that people have posted here.

Feel free to ask anymore questions. Wishing you the best!

text:
A long time ago now, I was at a restaurant with a friend. The young woman waiting on our table asked if we had any questions before ordering. I said "yes, what is the meaning of life?" And without hesitating, she replied:
"Good friends, good food, good conversations."
And I said, "good answer."

What is important to you in your life? For some it is money, or creativity, or not being stressed out, or living in the country away from crowds, or helping others, or raising good kids. Your money just goes elsewhere when you die. So do your things. Some say do what you love, and the money will follow. Maybe. There are plenty of struggling "artists." You can create online videos devoid of any value that get millions of views. You can throw the idea of morality out the window. You reap what you sow. You are the one who has to look at yourself in the mirror each day. The world is not fair. Never has been. And probably never will be based on the human DNA. Surround yourself with good people, not enablers. Understand that geo-political issues never go away and they will affect you. Do your research before moving. The internet is full of useful information from people who are local to the place that interests you. Ask lots of questions. There are plenty of people who have "been there done that." Though, in the case of some countries, their ability to communicate freely is severely restricted. 

I have never been to South Korea. But knowing how the work/life structure is there, it would not be the place for me, except for visiting as a traveler perhaps. Japan is similar in the work element. Death from overwork has a name there. Karoshi. Mental health help is sorely lacking. People just reach a breaking point after remaining silent for so long and they explode in major mental health breakdowns, many times in public.

Be a good example in life. Not a bad example of humanity. Help others, but don't ignore yourself. 

The history of various parts of the world is quite diverse and violent.  It has shaped many areas perspectives from generation to generation. 

What that woman at the restaurant said to me in response to my question, I sill remember decades later. To it I might add:
Good health, good family, good thoughts, and a good night's sleep. 

All work an no play makes other people and their inner circle rich.

Time off is good for you and your mental health and well being. 
You are in charge of you.

text: I was in Korea as a teacher for 5 years, and I would've stayed longer, but the city school district I was in changed their rules where foreign teachers had to change schools every 4 years just like the certified Korean teachers. The thing is though, I met and married my husband while in Korea, it's one reason I stayed so long, and he was working at a university, and the school district could have moved me to a school on the other side of the city, which was like almost 2 hours from where I was, my schools were on the other end. More than likely my husband would have had to commute to the university, or I could've taken the housing allowance and we live half way and we both commute. But neither of us really wanted to do that. And the pollution kept giving me sinus infections, even wearing a mask, and I had to go on antibiotics a few times, not good. And at the time the school district was reducing the amount of teachers because they were losing a but of their budget. And also, my visa being tied to my work was annoying, and I was no where near the amount of points needed to get an F2 visa. My school also didn't want me to change schools either, so they worked out a deal with the district to let me stay for a 5th year if I did not renew again. After 5 years, me and my husband moved to his home country and we've been here ever since. But if I hadn't have had to change schools, if the pollution wasn't making me sick, if  I had enough points to get an F2 visa, I think we would've stayed a lot longer, we both really liked it there.

text:
I've been an English teacher here in South Korea for five years. I was at one academy for three years from 2021 to 2023. Teaching here can be a coin flip. Some places are great to work, but many are terrible. It all comes down to management. I've worked in Daejeon, Uijeongbu, Dongtan, Anyang (2024), and Seoul at a new job (2025.) I also almost exclusively worked afternoon hours, from 1-8 or 9pm, which is a lot easier than morning jobs, which have longer hours and typically involve more work for equal pay.

Working and living in Seoul is the roughest, even though it's where most foreigners live and where most of the opportunities and highest paying jobs are. Seoul is also extremely discriminatory and pretty much only looks for attractive young women from the US, Canada, or Australia. If you don't fit this criteria, you very likely won't get hired in Seoul, unless the academy is really special or you're willing to be slave labor and work almost for free. This is one thing a lot of female foreign teachers never talk about, because it doesn't affect them, but most of the industry is female; about 65-70%. I'm not complaining about it, but if the genders were reversed, you know of lot of these same women _would_ be complaining about it, so Double Standards and all.

Honestly, anyone who considers themselves a "social media influencer" would not make a good teacher in South Korea. You can't be a self-absorbed person and expect to just glide by teaching in this country doing the bare minimum and putting in more work on YouTube and Instagram than you do for your actual job.

If anyone wants to teach in South Korea, I'd argue to NOT work in Seoul, but any other somewhat large city instead, like Suwon, Incheon, Osan, Dongtan, or even Busan (Korea's Los Angeles.) Most of the bad experiences of teaching in Korea comes from inexperienced people who worked for cheap in Seoul from 8:30am-6:30pm Monday through Friday for about $1,800 USD a month. I earn about 4 million won a month right now ($3,000 USD) working a new job in Daechi, Seoul, the upper-class part of the city, but that took about five years to get there and dozens of rejected emails.

text: It's important to note that the perception of low salaries often comes from foreigners who may not have professional qualifications. As a doctor and business owner, I can say that for those of us with experience, salaries are not necessarily low. I feel that many foreigners in Japan without a profession are the ones who face challenges. Currently, I’m living in the U.S., and I’ve noticed that grocery prices have risen significantly compared to three years ago. However, as a professional, this increase doesn’t affect me as much. I see many foreigners coming to the U.S. without qualified work experience who struggle and then say things like, “The American dream is a lie; I’m going back to my country.” But I believe that the issue often lies in not having a profession or specialized skills.My advice to anyone considering their career path is to pursue a degree that you are genuinely interested in and that will be useful in the job market. Specializing in a specific field can provide you with valuable skills that are in demand. While even those of us in the top 1% may feel economic pressures, the difference between being a specialized professional and someone offering general services is significant. In Japan, there are many professionals with their own businesses and relevant college degrees. Unfortunately, a large percentage of foreigners do not fall into this category. Those without education or specialized skills may find it difficult to earn a sustainable income. I do see specialized foreigners who speak Japanese working in high-paying jobs, but for those at the bottom who don’t speak the language, the job opportunities are limited, leading to lower salaries. The situation is similar in the U.S. Many people have neglected the importance of obtaining a good degree in traditional fields, resulting in those without qualifications facing the most struggles. I know many Korean doctors and nurses who are starting their medical careers in the U.S. and Japan due to challenges in the Korean medical system.Honestly, most of us are not struggling; we work hard but are compensated well enough to enjoy a comfortable life. For Japanese and Korean professionals, the work we do is not much different from what we would do in our home countries. This is why I believe that the Asian approach of obtaining a strong degree and becoming a professional is a wise choice. We don’t see ourselves as needing to rely on any country; we simply go out and work. Unfortunately, I don’t see a path for those without a solid educational background or profession in the U.S., Korea, or Japan. They are likely to struggle. I would advise against moving to Asia to seek jobs that don’t require a level of education, as it can lead to financial hardship. The same goes for low-paying professions that are undervalued. It's essential to be strategic about your life plan, not just in your own country but everywhere.

text:
I have a spooky travel story, a bit! I studied abroad in Sydney, Australia, and helped to come up with events and things for our group of students to do. I'm a big fan of Halloween so I coordinated a tour of Q Station (old quarantine island, used to quarantine people with illnesses like the plague) at 10pm and ending at midnight, on Halloween. 

It was a fascinating tour, very spooky, one of those places you're walking through and can just kinda feel the energy and history and the lives of the people who died there. It was VERY spooky. Going around at night, they give you lanterns so light is very limited, and you're just walking through old hospital rooms, gas chambers, and communal showers (that was honestly the scariest part of the whole tour). You're surrounded by trees and very little light. I think 5 people in our group left within the first fifteen minutes of the tour because they were too scared (needless to say this trip kind of made me very unpopular haha). Even if spooky night tours are not your thing, I'd really recommend a tour of Q island for the history. And you can see the stars really clearly there at night since there's little light pollution.

I've also had very spooky experiences in Savannah, GA (definitely do ghost tours there!), and in cabins in TN.

text:
I only spent a day in Seoul, but I had a great time. I think the best parts of it can eclipse Kyoto - I enjoyed the Palace and that cute neighborhood that surrounds it, plus the hill and greenery was oddly exactly the same as Kyoto. The local markets all across the city are really fun and remind me a bit of Mexico (in a good way). I love all the street vendors and cooks. People were very helpful and friendly to me - I accidentally couldn't pay for an express bus since I ran out of cash, so a local offered to swap my Japanese Yen for Korean Won so I could pay for the bus. The thoughtfulness was really nice. The cleanliness of the whole city, including the trains, was wonderful. I also liked the safety. Han Dynasty conquered large part of Korean Peninsula.
Jeong Yak Yong wrote in 아방강역고(Territory of My Country), "The land from the north of the Yeol river to the south of the Yalu river had been Han(漢) Dynasty's territory since Emperor Wu. The Yeol river is located in Seoul. The land north of the Yeol river was originally Han(漢) Dynasty's territory, so the river was a border between Han(漢) Dynasty and Samhan(三韓). Thus, people of Samhan(三韓) call this Yeol river as the Han river(漢江)."
Jeong Yak Yong was a philosopher and scientist in the 18th century. He was interested in Physics.
According to Jeong Yak Yong, Han Chinese conquered the land between the Yalu and the Han river. So the northern part of Seoul(where Cheongwadae and old palaces are located) was a Chinese territory about 2000 years ago. However, Gangnam wasn't a Chinese territory.

basically most of what is North Korea today, though half of them (the 2 southern ones closest to South Korea) were conquered by Koreans within 25 years and the northernmost one was pushed back to current-day China within 100 years or so. It's interesting to see parallels with the Roman presence in Britain: virtually the same time period and duration (both around 400 years from around the beginning of the first millennium) and similar territorial pattern (half the peninsula, half the island).

The main commandery, Lelang, existed for 400 years. That was in present day North Korea. There is archeological and written evidence for the commanderies.

Another interesting tidbit is that one of the three Samhan, Jinhan, claimed that it was founded by Qin dynasty refugees.

In fact, Park Hyeokgose's mother was supposed to be Chinese royalty who fled to Jinhan..

text:
@dearcoolz You are seriously twisting history to fit a narrative. Yes, the Han Dynasty briefly set up commanderies like Lelang after defeating Wiman Joseon in 108 BCE, but those were colonial outposts, not signs of full Chinese control over the Korean Peninsula. These outposts were short-lived and limited in scope, and Korean kingdoms like Goguryeo quickly pushed them out.

Jeong Yak Yong was an 18th century scholar reflecting on historical texts from his time, not a modern historian. Quoting him as if his interpretation is absolute fact is misleading. He lived in a time when access to archeological evidence was limited and China was seen as the cultural center of Asia.

The land between the Yalu and Han rivers was contested territory, not stable Han Dynasty land. It is absurd to claim that Seoul or the Korean heartland was Chinese territory. That would be like claiming Britain is Roman today because Rome ruled parts of it 2000 years ago.

And as for Samhan or Jinhan being influenced by Qin refugees, that does not prove Chinese conquest. Migration happened across all regions. That is not the same as colonization.

The truth is Korea has thousands of years of independent history. It fought off invasions from Tang, Yuan, Ming, Qing, and Japan, and maintained its own dynasties, language, culture, and borders. You are cherry-picking fragments and ignoring the overwhelming historical record that shows Korea was never fully conquered by China. Just stop pushing that narrative and spreading misinformation.

text:
⁠Stop pushing that narrative and spreading misinformation. You are seriously twisting history to fit a narrative. Yes, the Han Dynasty briefly set up commanderies like Lelang after defeating Wiman Joseon in 108 BCE, but those were colonial outposts, not signs of full Chinese control over the Korean Peninsula. These outposts were short-lived and limited in scope, and Korean kingdoms like Goguryeo quickly pushed them out.

Jeong Yak Yong was an 18th century scholar reflecting on historical texts from his time, not a modern historian. Quoting him as if his interpretation is absolute fact is misleading. He lived in a time when access to archeological evidence was limited and China was seen as the cultural center of Asia.

The land between the Yalu and Han rivers was contested territory, not stable Han Dynasty land. It is absurd to claim that Seoul or the Korean heartland was Chinese territory. That would be like claiming Britain is Roman today because Rome ruled parts of it 2000 years ago.

And as for Samhan or Jinhan being influenced by Qin refugees, that does not prove Chinese conquest. Migration happened across all regions. That is not the same as colonization.

The truth is Korea has thousands of years of independent history. It fought off invasions from Tang, Yuan, Ming, Qing, and Japan, and maintained its own dynasties, language, culture, and borders. You are cherry-picking fragments and ignoring the overwhelming historical record that shows Korea was never fully conquered by China.

Welcome to Korea guys! 

Some motels give you big towels, but not all do. At ours, we usually use small towels a couple of times (depends on the person), and then wash them straight away — so it’s all good! Even though I live in Australia, I still use small towels and wash them often.

text:
A few things I just wanted to explain while watching video.

- What you found in motel room is descending life line, which you can use to escape in case of fire. I think government law force them to place them in each room, make it visible or something. 
- Convenient store things are a little pricey as they operate 24/7 and they are pretty much everywhere. You can buy better drinks in cheap cafe and they are not DIY. (But it will be still cheap enough for most people imo. In tourist spots, convenient store will be cheaper option compared to other places as well)
- Weather in Korea is extremely hot and humid during Summer and cold in Winter. Best time to probably visit is April~June and September~November. 
- Busan is city that's known to have worst driver (not badly skilled, but shitty ones). It might be from perception, but you all saw how road is like over there. 
- Public Safety warning have 3 different types, and as you pointed out, one of them sends very trivial messages frequently, so people usually turn that off.

text:
How were they rude? I guess I can imagine old people living out in a remote rural place might seem rude to outsiders, because they are probably fearful. Living in the UK, I think I can imagine older people in the countryside wouldn't exactly be open and delighted if meeting a foreigner who especially looked different to them and did not speak English easily. I don't want to say they'd be purposefully rude, but definitely fearful I think, they'd be wary. Old people don't feel as confident, they can't protect themselves as easily as young men, and they get taken advantage of a lot. 

Also just being real, they're more likely to have grown up in their rural village if it's in England, and speaking just from my perspective, they don't like influxes of new people into a village they knew from being children, especially "foreigners" settling there. Older people are more likely to be conservative, again, they are wary, and they resent a village or town that was their home starting to look totally different, culturally, to the point of being unrecognisable. 

Obviously that's an English perspective, but I suspect there's stuff in common with Korea, given how radically that country has been expected to adapt to cultural change.

text:
In Korea, it’s very difficult to fire employees, so once someone joins a company, they often stay there for decades. At first, this might sound like a good thing, but the downside is that companies are extremely cautious when hiring.

That’s why Korean students study so hard to get into good companies from the very beginning. Korean companies also tend to be reluctant to hire foreigners, because they assume foreigners are less likely to stay with the company long-term.

As a result, foreigners are often pushed out by Korean candidates and have a hard time getting into good jobs in Korea.

There is also a huge gap between different levels of workplaces in Korea. Large corporations offer much better salaries, benefits, and overall treatment, while small and medium-sized companies often offer far worse pay, benefits, and working conditions. This kind of gap exists everywhere, of course, but it is especially severe in Korea.

For example, my company is relatively large, and at 5 p.m. the computers automatically lock, making it impossible to continue working. On the other hand, a friend of mine who works at a small company has to work overtime very frequently.

The point is that foreigners, who are usually outcompeted by Koreans for positions at large companies, tend to end up working at smaller companies with poorer conditions. As a result, their work experience in Korea is often not very good.

text:
My take on negative aspect of living in Korea from an ex-Korean point of view (I lived in South Korea during my growing years, but have moved to the US since then):

1. If personal space (both physical and psychological) is high up in your list of priorities, then you might want to consider a different country.

2. Koreans tend to be too materialistic and superficial, so keep this in mind. (For example, the conspicuous display of one's social status is a big deal in Korea.)

3. Discrimination is widespread: gender, wealth, academic standing, etc. To add insult to injury, if you are being discriminated, you will most likely to be blamed and it can be quite a struggle to find someone who is willing to understand your grievances.

4. Koreans can be very nosy and double-faced: i.e., While pretending to be nice, they can smear your image when talking to others behind your back. This means you must maintain some distance between yourself and folks around you, including both you co-workers and even the rest of your household.

5. Before moving to Korea, make sure to do a plenty of research in order to build up a more accurate mental picture of the said country. The kind of Korea social media influencers, tourism and entertainment industries would like to portray is very different from the reality. In particular, study South Korea's socioeconomic problems and their underlying causes.

네가 우리 사회를 '디스토피아'라 생각할 수 있는 이유는, 역설적으로 우리 나라가 여유가 있기 때문일 것이야.

세상에는 기본적인 의식주,인권이 보장되지 못하는 국가가 정말 많아.

유럽,아메리카에도 그런 나라가 많은데, 아시아로 범위를 한정하면 그 비율은 더욱 심하겠지.

이런 국가들은 기본적인 의식주가 보장되지 못하고,

공무원이 부패해 일을 똑바로 안하고,

노동 강도가 심해 인간을 기계처럼 다룬다거나,

아니면 아예 태업을 해 국가 생산성이 지극히 낮다거나,

정부가 독재를 해 국민들을 탄압한다거나....

여러 양상이 있을거야.


그런 국가가 몇개 있을까? 저런 예시에 해당하는 국가가 몇개일까?

내 생각에 저 예시에 해당하지 않는 국가보다 해당되는 국가가 훨씬 훨씬 많을거야.


내가 생각하는 한국 생활의 장점은 바로 "사회 복지제도"야.

외국인들은 kpop이니, 드라마니 하는데 솔직히 나는 그런거 관심이 없거든...

그런데 한국 생활의 정말 큰 좋은점은 바로 이 사회복지제도가 잘 자리잡혀 있다는거야.


 전국의 학교에 양질의 식사를 무료로 제공하고(네가 유튜브에서 볼 수 있는 한국 점심 영상 중 고등학교 점심은 거의 무료이고, 대학의 경우 4~6$에 한끼를 할 수 있다)

가정 형편이 뒤떨어지는 아이들에게 교육의 기회를 제공하고(대학교 장학금, 무상 학비 제도)

낮은 교통비를 보장해 형편이 없는 자들에게 이동의 권리가 침해되지 않도록 하고...
(지하철로 대도시 반경 70~100km 거리를 1$로 이동하는 것이 가능한 것 처럼)


이 모든게 내가 생각하는 한국 복지 제도의 장점들이야.

어떤 근거로 그렇게 생각하냐고? 내가 특수한 가정환경에 속해 저런 혜택을 받고 살아왔거든.

나는 저런 혜택을 받고 살아왔기에, 우리 나라에 정말 감사해. 

내가 미국이나 중국의 빈민층으로 태어났으면 과연 지금처럼 교육을 받고,무료 학교 식사를 할 수 있었을까?

대학교엔 갈 수 있었을까?

 내가 좋아하는 역사책을 학교 도서관에서 무료로 읽을 수 있었을까?

아마 못 그랬을것이야.

나는 🇨🇳-🇰🇷 혼혈이라 중국에서도 살고, 한국에서도 살아봤어.

중국에 갔다오고 느낀 점은? 정말 한국에서 태어난 것이 다행이라는 사실이었어.

중국 정도면 해외에서는 수준 높은 아시아 국가되는 편이야. 훌륭한 문화와 강한 군대와 국력...그리고 역사

근데 실제 시민들의 삶은 어떨까?

상상 이상으로 힘들어. 평균적인 임금은 러시아와 비슷한데, 물가는 한국이나 대만 등과 비슷하다고 느낄 때가 있어.

9 to 9라는 지옥같은 출근문화, 그리고 높은 집값, 과도한 교육열 등...

정치 사상의 탄압같은걸 제쳐봐도, 일단 국민들의 평균적인 행복이 보장되지 못하는 것 같았어.

아시아에서 가장 강한 국가인 중국이 그런데, 다른 국가는 어떨까?

생각건대 🇯🇵 🇹🇼 🇸🇬 등의 선진국을 빼면 상황이 크게 낫지는 않을 것이야.


너가 인간의 정신적 가치를 강조하잖아?

그런데 하나 생각해보자.

생활 수준이 높은데 정신적 가치는 뒤떨어지는 국가는 있어도,

 생활 수준이 낮은데 정신적 가치는 높은, 그러한 나라가 얼마나 있을까?

미국, 영국과같은 전통적 선진국에서 빈곤층의 노숙 문제와 반 이민 폭력 시위 같은 것이 문제가 되는 마당인데, 

소득 수준이 낮은 국가는 어떨까? 아마 더 심할 것이야.

소득 수준이 낮으면 사회 보장 제도를 실시할 수 없고, 그러면 최하층 사람들의 가치는 무시된다고.


동의해?

I agree with you, my friend. So sorry you had bad experiences there. The truth is, that they care so much about how other people think, let alone ‘foreigners’ especially the ‘superior’ white people. I personally don’t recommend South Korea at all. They have the highest suicide rates amongst OECD countries and the lowest birth rates. They bully each other since kindergarten based on wealth (a form of classism) up until someone commits su*cide. 

South Koreans are shallow, pretentious, materialistic, obsessed with lookism and extremely judgmental and discriminating. South Korea was one of the poorest countries after the 6.25 Korean war and then with dictatorships, the economy developed exponentially but the development of ‘civil awareness’ and ‘empathy’ was underdeveloped in comparison. Thus it resulted in creating so many sociopaths. 

Personally I avoid South Koreans at all costs. Especially the native ones. Whether you’re rich or poor, doesn’t matter. If you ain’t white, they will discriminate you and try to ruin your life out of jealousy (if they think you’re better at something than them) or simply because you’re different. Even if they are nice to your face, they are 99.9% talking behind your back, about your looks, non-conformism (lack of individuality; going against their Confucianist values), social status and etc, anything they can find flaws/weaknesses. 

A good example is this Korean who left multiple comments above because they are insecure about facing truths. They are busy sweeping every truths under the rug. They have to look perfect like KPOP. They try to ‘fix’ your honest ‘opinions’ because everyone has to love South Korea no matter what, due to their low self-esteem. Also the reason why so many celebs commit suicide because cancel culture is normalised here. I’m South Korean myself by the way, born and raised in European country. But I have also lived in Seoul for many years. Worked for some Korean companies. There are too many times South Koreans either tried to use me/scam me/bully me. Like I mentioned above. Avoid them and trash them. 

There’s a proverb in Korean 사촌이 땅을 사면 배아프다 which means ‘My stomach aches when my cousin purchases a land’. They are the most unhappy, jealous and insecure people I’ve met. This stems from the generational, national trauma from experiencing wars but South Koreans are on the next level. They are like bunch of hyenas. They are really the worst kind of people. They create derogatory/racist words all the time. I’m 검머외 (derogatory term for 2nd generation immigrant Koreans) meaning dark haired foreigner. Why did they create this word? Because they are jealous that we have escaped their hell-hole.

text:
Many South Koreans who have lived in Western countries as expatriates or students often faced difficult moments due to being foreigners. Invisible racial discrimination and cultural differences occasionally made them unhappy. However, they had to accept this, as they understood the saying, "When in Rome, do as the Romans do." Westerners in South Korea face similar challenges. If they cannot adapt to the social atmosphere and traditional customs of these foreign nations, they should consider leaving to avoid unnecessary psychological conflicts. 

As time has passed, the number of foreigners from diverse nationalities in South Korea has been increasing rapidly. Some Koreans believe that effective measures are needed to manage this influx. South Korea has traditionally been a nation-state with a single ethnic group, but the settlement process for foreigners is happening faster than expected. While South Korea is not a utopia, many Western visitors have unrealistic expectations about the country. It is important for visitors from Western countries to be objective. Despite living in South Korea, 80% of South Koreans feel that they are not happy.

ADOR kind of presented the apology as “however long it takes”, which might just be a way to not put a set timeline on anything, but it could also imply that some level of acceptance is conditional (aka you cannot resume idol activities until you apologize to X, Y, Z in A, B, and/or C ways, AND they are accepted by said persons).

What do you think New Jeans ‘concept’ will be if they resume activities? A big part of their appeal concept-wise was “girl next door type who enjoys being with friends and dancing casually”, it was very focused on innocence and an easygoing nature. Will ADOR continue with this same concept that, while wildly popular (even currently as they still chart well), feels disingenuous to many kpop fans? Or will they switch to a new concept? If they switch to a new concept, what will happen to all those demos and whatnot that they were preparing during New Jeans hiatus, maybe saved for the next group (like how BP supposedly used old 2NE1 songs)?

And lastly (maybe going to a bit of a slippery slope in my thoughts), why not just dungeon New Jeans? I know ADOR is all about money I’m sure they’re running cost analysis and earning potential calculations like crazy, but you think about the amount of rehab that will go into changing public opinion, the risk that it won’t even work and you have to try to engage a whole new audience, possibly changing their concept…why not just focus on a new group? Especially if, as I mentioned above, their return is contingent on the acceptance of the apology, then ADOR could theoretically keep them in limbo for a long time. (Again, I know this one is really my wildest thought with no basis, but it’s mainly based on the idea that New Jeans will have a very difficult time returning with the same image as they did when they first debuted)

Hey love, thank you for sharing this and allowing yourself to be vulnerable with us. It takes so much strength and courage to open your heart like that, and I (like so many others) truly appreciate you for it.

Grief is love’s final act, a testament to all the love you poured into someone, the love you still carry, but can no longer give in the same way. It’s that unspent love, all the moments you still wish you could share, the words you didn’t get to say. So when you miss him, when your heart aches, know that it's love speaking loud and clear. And I truly believe he’s watching over you, rooting for you on every step of the way.
I’m truly grateful that you’re surrounded by the love and support you so deeply deserve from your boyfriend and those closest to you, please remember to be gentle with yourself through it all. Healing takes time, and you deserve kindness from others, but most importantly, from yourself 🤍

text:
You had never lived on your own.  Anywhere you would have moved to and become independant, you would have met someobody there and fallen inlove.  It's a shame you had to move so far away  and fall in love there, because now you are tricking yourself to stay in Korea.  You are only stay because of your boyfriend.  

My advice for anybody who does not have much experience in life and relationships, to NOT move abroad.  If you want to move, move to another city in your country, and gain that experience.  Never let 'love' dictate your life.   This is especially so if you are very close to your family and friends.  Moving so far away from them and not returning just because you fell in love from the country you moved to, is stupid.  The time in your life when you will meet more people of the other sex is when you are young.  So if you move to China, for example, of course you'll meet some guy you like there, and that would turn to love.  But it also would have happened if you would have moved to another city in your own country or if you had moved to a nearby country, in this case, from Switzerland to France.  Why make life harder for yourself by moving so far away hwen you are so young and inexperienced?  And I say this from experience.  I have regrets and as a much older person, this is my advice to young men and women who move to other countries because they think they are 'fun' or 'cool', without ever considering the longterm complications.  You are only young once, and the time lost with your family and friends, will never be regained.

If you are much older and have experienced relationships and living on your own, well that's different.

text: I’m from India, from a middle-class family. I was introverted, an average student. After high school, I wanted to study abroad—not for luxury or showing off, but for space, independence, and a chance to build a different life. We chose Russia because it was affordable and realistic for my family. I wasn’t good at math; I only liked biology, and since my elder brother was already a doctor, from around ninth grade the direction of my life was more or less decided for me. I entered a small medical university in Russia and started medicine in English. That first year was one of the hardest years of my life. I faced a lot of isolation and discrimination—not only from locals, but even from my own countrymen. I’m from South India, I look different, and I don’t speak Hindi, and that alone was enough to make me feel like I didn’t belong. I also didn’t know Russian, my religion was different, and culturally I felt out of place everywhere. Slowly, I stopped feeling like a student and started feeling like a problem that didn’t fit anywhere. Over time, medicine stopped feeling like a dream and started feeling like a comparison. Every step felt measured against my brother. I didn’t hate studying; I hated who I was becoming while studying it. So I left medicine. I moved to Moscow, did a full year of Russian language studies, and changed my major. Around that same time, my health started deteriorating and I was diagnosed with a chronic genetic condition—something that doesn’t just “go away” and that forces you to rethink how you plan your life. I still continued, entered the new program, and tried to keep going while managing my health. My grades weren’t good, and later I was told to repeat a semester. Each semester cost around $3,500, and I knew what that money meant to my family. I didn’t want to sink deeper into a system I already felt disconnected from, especially with my health unstable, so I made the decision to quit. That decision caused a big fight at home, and I won’t pretend I handled that phase well. All my friends were graduating, getting jobs, and moving forward, while I was 22, back home, without a bachelor’s degree, without a clear identity, and without a story that sounded good. There was a very dark period mentally—not because life was impossible, but because I couldn’t see where I fit inside it anymore. One of the few things that genuinely helped me during that time was my faith. I’m not saying this to preach, but because it’s true: when my plans, confidence, and direction collapsed, having something bigger than my achievements to hold onto kept me grounded. Right now, I’m at home, I’m on treatment, and I’m not pretending to have everything figured out. I’m reflecting, stabilizing my health, and trying to understand my life instead of running from it.

I was scared of socializing with my younger peers, with facing a thesis I had no idea what I would do with, the financial burden their required immersion trip would set on my family, and the fears of what comes after graduation. At some point I also reached that epiphany while listening to career paths during company caravans, I couldn't quite picture myself in the roles they needed. I also couldn't imagine myself winning over all these talented and overachieving younger peers. Two major tragedies happened before and during my last semester in that program and the way one professor couldn't find it in her heart to just give a small extension I was begging for in the middle of my uncle's wake just snapped the last strand. She was always sick and on leave for whatever reason and we all just laughed it off despite her subjects being very important. That she couldn't even grant that while I, who wasn't very social, was begging her in a class chat which I'm usually too embarrassed to even ask questions in. It might be too entitled to have expected her to just say yes to my request but something about that moment just felt like a dose of cold water. It was a culmination of my fears and the final 'oh' that I could one day become that person if I stayed on this path. I actually had the chance to just transfer schools and finish my degree elsewhere, but I couldn't convince myself I was ready to jump back into this program. There's a school right across us that's more expensive but notoriously easy to graduate from but I saved myself that last bit of dignity and pride, and just moved to a different path. Maybe one day I'll see if my credits are still valid and finish it to prove something to myself but for now I've found a nicer environment for my mental health. It's devastating to realize your plans are wrong and to accept defeat over wrong decisions and time wasted, but something about getting kicked out of my program felt like a weight of my soul. The guilt of seeing what your peers have achieved, what you are unable to do, the realizations of the what ifs, and the utter shame are the hardest part but the strength to move on is something I never thought my weak minded self would ever be capable of. text: ​@sandyspace_ytThird World is an outdated term that originated during the Cold War as a political term, and had nothing to do with economy, but evolved to become a shorthand for "backwards," "underdeveloped," etc. It is both offensive, and inaccurate, because the world economy has evolved much since the term was coined, and today is far more complex and doesn't allow for dividing the world into two. The term "Third World" reduces diverse nations with varied cultures, economies, and histories to a single negative stereotype, reinforcing outdated and simplistic views. I know you didn't mean it that way, but it's best to be aware of it and choose a different term. It's best not to use any labels because each country is complex, but if you have to explain then you might rather choose "low-income country" or "developing country." They're not perfect either, but much better than "Third World."

text: Sandy - I dropped out of college as a senior. I wasn't mentally there. I was going through a tough break-up and fell hard into depression. I joined the military. After one year in the Army, I went back to school. I earned my BA in computer science. I still stayed in the military. I'm about to retire in the Army. I use to believe that there was one path in life. Now, I believe there are opportunities in any path, even if you walked off the trail for awhile. Every new chance of experience I got, I took it. Without a doubt, I was able to learn new things and gain so much experience. I too was born in a third world country. I was born in a refugee camp. If I'm able to overcome my adversity, you can too.  As you get older, you will realize that how people see you means little. I'm 42 now, my health is the most important thing. I know it's hard to do as a young woman, as a young inexperience person. Time heals all and experience requires time. I hope all is well and I wish you the best.

But after 10 years, I realise if I wanted to see other places, it was a good time to do it because I was still young enough to have this energy and old enough to have a decent salary. Since 2021 I've been working remotely and travelling veeeeeery slow, spending lots of time home at my parents house, or where my friends live, or just wherever I'm curious about (I spent 2 months in Korea for 3 consecutive years btw ❤). I always feel it's important to me to point out I didn't leave because of London, never cried harder when my flatmates and I left out house after 7 years living together... but sometimes you know a hard choice is the right choice for you! text:
Hey Adrienne! I recently made the decision to move back to America, and it's crazy how much your experiences line up with mine. I moved to Seoul when I turned 18 and I left about six and a half years later. I never experienced adulthood in the US either, and just like you, I've faced tons of comments from people in my life. They're baffled by my decision to leave such a comfortable country, especially at a time like this, when the US is in absolute turmoil. 

I love Korea so much, and I could definitely continuing living happily there. But I got the itch to explore, get out of my comfort zone, and live a new life. I also want to experience dating people who speak the same language as me (something I found out is very important to me is having no language barrier between my partner and myself). I want to try living in a country where people are more open about mental health. Plus there are better career prospects for my field in LA. 

So yeah, I want to try being an American, as uncomfortable as it is. It has been so hard dealing with new things like the shitty US health care system, which I never experienced. I remind myself sometimes that if things don't work out in the states, I could always move back to Korea. It's not like we're barred from the country once we lose our 외국인등록증s lol.

But yeah, I'm wishing you all the best! It's such a major decision that I'm glad you were able to make.
