text: As a Korean American who has similar conversations with my cousins from Korea, this was an interesting conversation. Yes, Korean culture can be toxic. However, as an American, is American culture any better? Are Americans actually happier? There are also a ton of Americans struggling financially and trying to hustle and survive. The younger generation in America is also struggling with limited job opportunities, debt, high housing prices, and mental health issues. I know the focus was on Korea, but I don't think it's fair to just demonize Korean culture and elevate Western cultures. It's not about judging which one is better or worse but point out the good and the bad in every culture.  I think there's a way that we can lionize American and Western cultures while only focusing on the toxic parts of Korean culture. It just needs to be more balanced. Moreover, Tammy was the most thoughtful and eloquent speaker. She actually listened and referenced the words of the other people in the group. On the other hand, Kelsey kept interrupting and also just spewed her own opinions judgmentally without trying to listen to other perspectives. Also, maybe this is just me as an American, but viewing things from places of power and privilege, Kelsey just came off as very privileged and thus could easily dismiss the views of the other people. While there are people struggling financially and trying to survive, she was proud of how she could sleep in and choose what she wants to do. That is not an option for many young people in both Korea and the US. That was a major turnoff in this conversation. Even though I agreed with many of the things Kelsey said, the way she was judgmental, dismissive, and arrogant in the conversation was distracting. In the end, I appreciated the conversation and hope you have more thoughtful places of dialogue and different viewpoints about life in Korea.

text:
The South African mindset is a bit reversed.  You graduate from University, work for various large corporate companies in your field, build up experience and contacts, then become an entrepreneur.   Once you understand how an industry ticks, it's easier to find a gap in the market.  

Other options our young people have, is to leave SA after Uni and gain experience in Europe, UK or USA, etc then return and bring that knowledge and experience home!  

Regarding marriage, I can understand the mindset of young people to marry later than for example my generation did.  Yet, in SA those standards are still going.  People are getting married in their droves, after Uni.  Perhaps South Africans are contented with less material wealth as they begin in life, then build a life together.  The mindset is two is better than one.  It's a very personal choice.  My advice to my children is, there is no train to catch concerning marriage. From 25 for women and 30 for men in my opinion is a healthy age.  

Perhaps the Korea education system and societal values makes it a complex topic.  Now that I think about it, my daughter is 23.  I got married at 22.  😂 She is still enjoying her life, attending rugby matches, music shows etc.  I can not imagine my life without my hubby even at that young age.  We still have a lot of laughs and enjoy life together. If it's the right person, you can't go wrong!  ❤. South Africans love children, it caters well for childcare and healthy education.  School is a blast, because there are fo many festivals and fun stuff happening, it's a hub of vibrance and life.  It's sad to notice what us happening in SK.  Your youth is so precious, you should enjoy it!  It breaks my heart a little.  Marriage is a wonderful thing, family is precious.

From a parent's perspective I agree.  While you are young, just carry on studying, build your life and your finance, pay off your debt, live simply!

With all the controversies going on in SA at the moment, race baced laws, refugee status for Afrikaners, it's obvious that the world is also finally taking notice of SA post appartheid.  It's such a beautiful country, with so much potential, we're sitting on diamonds and gold that doesn't get mined properly etc.  Lots of frustrations!  BUT we plug and play!

🇯🇵 Japan: 45-min lunch(often not guaranteed), personal phone use almost banned
🇺🇸 USA: 30–40 min lunch, limited phone use during work

📌 Korea, Japan, USA: Work Hours Compared
🇯🇵 Japan: ~1,600 hrs/year (~200+ hrs/year unpaid overtime hidden, no severance pay)

🇰🇷 Korea: ~1,900 hrs/year (full 1-hour lunch break, no work during lunch)

Abe’s 1億総活躍社会 fooled no one: it was statistical acrobatics to make underemployment look like prosperity.

text: Good videos.  Was in Seoul June-July 2025.  In 2023 was in Suwon, Seoul and Daegu.  The last 3 days in Seoul this year  were extremely hot and humid - reminded me of Houston or Florida.  The subway system is INCREDIBLY clean - there are not even many garbage cans around.  Anyone from New York, Chicago or a city with a subway system in the US will appreciate that.  The air conditioning - as you mentioned - works very well, unlike some subway cars in the US.  People are very polite and as a polite person myself I really like that.  In major US cities people can be very rude.  I am older and noticed the kids speak surprisingly good English.  The only thing different I could think of is maybe more access to English via the internet and television these days compared to the 70s or 80s.  Thanks for your videos.  Entertaining and educational.  As far as food goes, I have to disagree a bit about the food.  I have gout so I avoid eating meat.  Luckily for me the food options in Korea are so varied that I have many non-meat dishes to choose from.  There are many excellent tofu-based and seafood-based meals as well as just straight up vegetable dishes.  Not only that, it is a lot of fun because there many vegetables and/or roots available in Korea that are not sold in the US.  So at times it is a bit of a culinary adventure, which I enjoy a lot.

🌳 Massive riverside parks (Han River, Seokchon Lake, Cheonggyecheon), forests, and hiking trails (Bukhansan, Inwangsan) — nature seamlessly integrated into urban life.
🛍 Premium malls (Lotte World Mall, COEX, The Hyundai Seoul), vibrant street markets (Gwangjang, Namdaemun), and multicultural districts (Itaewon, Dongdaemun, Seorae Village).
🎨 Cultural hubs (Seoul Arts Center, DDP, Gwanghwamun Square), hanok cafes, themed cafes, and wellness jjimjilbangs — uniquely Korean experiences.
🎢 Lotte World and VR theme parks inside the city — amusement without needing to leave Seoul.
🍜 From traditional food stalls to Michelin-starred restaurants — culinary diversity unmatched.
🎮 E-sports, PC bangs, karaoke coin rooms — more immersive and vibrant than Japan.
🌆 Even Seoul’s suburbs feel alive, with high-rises, vibrant streets, and mixed-use neighborhoods where daily life seamlessly blends work, leisure, and culture.

➡️ Seoul is alive everywhere — not just around train stations.

🔴 Tokyo? A consumption city hyped by numbers.
🏚 Beyond the station hubs, 90% of Tokyo spreads out as endless rows of low-rise, two-story houses with no shops, cafes, or street life. Cities built for silence, not vibrancy.
🏠 Narrow streets tangled with utility poles and scarce greenery hint at a city trapped under its shiny surface.
🎰 Pachinko pulls ¥14T ($130B) a year, addicting 3.6% of adults (500,000 people) and wrecking lives with debt and broken families.
🎮 Akihabara game centers = repetitive and outdated.
🍺 Shibuya bars = slightly different themes, same drinking culture.
⚠JK business(Kabukicho, Ikebukuro), fetishized AV culture, underage sex trade hidden beneath the surface
🏰 Suburban Tokyo leans on Disneyland for entertainment — a symptom of the lack of diversity in the city itself.
👜 Ginza, Omotesando, Azabudai Hills = luxury shopping streets, but department stores keep shutting down (Shinjuku Alta, Odakyu Myload, Tokyu Shibuya).

➡️ “Tokyo is bigger.” Sure. So is a desert. 😂

🏆 Verdict:
Seoul = dynamic, immersive, and the heart of K-culture ❤️
Tokyo = an illusion of “things to see,” inflated by Japanophiles(Wapanese)

text:
16:51 As a Korean who was born and raised in Korea (and now living abroad), I totally relate to how she sees Korean society. To me, Korea is kind of going through a transitional period. We’ve achieved such rapid and impressive economic growth, but honestly, our reflection on life, community, and culture hasn’t really caught up yet. At this stage, I don’t think we need more “development” or bigger achievements. Instead, maybe it’s time to pause and look back at what we might’ve missed while we were chasing economic success.

One thing I’ve noticed is that family self-interest runs really deep in Korea. Many people basically think their family is the only group really worth caring about. After college, it’s rare to see people willing to invest time or effort into friendships—they see it as a waste. There’s not much interest in building true, lifelong friendships that bring real joy. And I’m not talking about sticking with friends just out of "의리" or nostalgia, but actually putting in the effort to stay connected and care for each other over time.

I really think we need to pay more attention to the emotional and cultural richness we’ve been missing out on—like generosity, a smile, and being less judgmental. I love my country and I’m unconditionally proud of it. I truly believe Korea will get through this transition in an amazing way.

And one more thing!
To everyone interested in Korea, thank you and welcome!🫶🇰🇷

text:
3:59 To the girl considering Malaysia as an option for a master's degree, please PLEASE don't. I've done my bachelor's and master's in Malaysia (biotechnology) and graduated from the top university in the country with a CGPA of 4.0, but I couldn't find a job, not even decent internships. And btw, education here is overrated and not that good for all majors. Like, I've noticed engineering degrees have a better education here compared to my major. For example, in my bachelor's degree, the vast majority of the subjects were theoretical and we had very few lab sessions for a major that requires hands on skills like biology. And obviously, I didn't even get the chance to get such skills from a proper training or a job. The law here is strictly against hiring foreigners unless they have something very special or a very special experience abroad. Throughout my stay here in Malaysia, I've only heard of one of my foreign colleagues landing a job at a company! Only ONE! The rest of the foreign workers here that I know of are either university professors (which means I have to suffer with a PhD degree, which is what I had to do unfortunately), or people with blue collar jobs who either have UN card (UN refugees) or work illegally and have to be thrown in the jail for a few days whenever caught by authorities. The salaries here aren't that good either. Renewing a visa is becoming harder and more expensive, and no matter how long you live here, you won't get the nationality and a long term residency is quite pricey and has lots of conditions. I personally know a person who lived for 14 years in Malaysia and then moved to Korea. After 4 years in Korea, he achieved what he couldn't achieve in Malaysia for 14 years. 

All in all, Malaysia is a good tourist destination and has lots of advantages, but I won't recommend it to anyone for studying or working.

Whoever is considering moving abroad for studying, if you don't plan to go back to your country right after graduation, then you better study in a country that has more lenient laws for hiring foreigners and at least gives you 1 year of visa after graduation for job hunting.

text:
I've lived long-term in four different countries, each with its own culture, language, and religion—spread across different continents. I studied, learned the language, and worked in almost all of them. I only passed through Korea once—just a stopover in Seoul. I remember Korean Air’s lounge had those near-flatbed seats, but that’s as far as I got. In that region, I’ve spent more time in Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia, and Laos. I’ve also briefly visited or transited through Cambodia, Myanmar, Shanghai, Taiwan, and Hong Kong—some of them multiple times. Expat stories are always fascinating, especially the challenges people face—I’ve had my share, for sure.

I recently watched a video by a researcher analyzing behavioral shifts in people under 35. He suggested there's almost a species-level divide—big differences in empathy, emotional expression, and how people communicate. You bring up empathy in your videos, and according to his findings, that’s exactly what’s missing in many younger people today. Communication tends to be clipped, flat, and detached—very different from older generations. If you're feeling lost, like you mentioned in another video, maybe it’s because you relate more emotionally to people over 35—who tend to express more, feel more, and connect more deeply.

For some reason, I really like your videos and content—there’s something genuine about the way you share things. You’re definitely not alone. A lot of people are struggling to make sense of the shifts happening in society right now. Just keep being yourself, but move through things with a bit more caution. You’ve got a likable presence, and that goes a long way.

text:
Similar experience. I became a landlord out of necessity during the financial crisis after yet another transcontinental move to start another expat job. I knew nothing about the legality of letting so I commissiioned a property management company. They are completely schizoid because they represent landlord as well as tenant rights and I kept getting demands for this and that stuff that needs fixing. Anyway it paid the mortgage and hanging on to the property for almost 10 yearrs returned a very small gain but luckily no loss compared to the purchase price. The first tenant went on vacation during a -25 deg C cold snap. The property management company didn't even know that they'd gone and they switched of the heating completely so not even a minimum warming level was set. The house turned into a goldfish ball because the attic watertank valve burst. I was going to sue the property management company for negligience but accepted the advise to cut my losses for the legal system would most likely protect that company. After all the landlord house insurance coughed up 50 grand pound Sterling for the internal renovation and loss of rental income on top of that etc. 

I have since then given up being an international landlord and just let out another appartment locally. The walkabouts are a necessity. 

Life is most cruel. It took me a long time to heal after the above episode but it made me more resilient. Fortunately I suffered possible financial losses overall and some mental trauma but I am still alive. 

A week in silence in Taize followed by one of the Camino routes to the Cathedral de Santiago de Compostela degaussed my brain and recharged my batteries. 

Life is short! We need to live it and most importantly enjoy it.

text:
@thanGacaoI think this may also be a relative thing. On the expat FB groups I see lots of Americans usually complaining about Korean driving and yet in almost two years of driving in Korea I've never had any problems whatsoever (knock on wood). My perception is Korean drivers are often aggressive but are totally predictable. There is a pattern to their driving, they telegraph what they're going to do, it's very much a predictable pattern. For example: Korean drivers won't let you in unless you "nose in" somewhat aggressively but if you do, they let you in. There are lots of standard moves they make and it only took me a few days of driving to pick up on most of them. By contrast, back in the US, drivers might be less aggressive but they're also way more unpredictable. Some drive predictably but then some drive weirdly slowly, or block passing, or cut over suddenly with no warning, or... so many different patterns. I find drivers who drive super sluggishly even more dangerous than aggressive drivers because they might do things like stop suddenly when they don't need to or block the flow of traffic sometimes causing accidents, etc.

In Korea by contrast people mostly seem to follow similar patterns, and while taxi drivers are more aggressive I don't have trouble reading what they're going to do.

3:41 You have managed to give me the vocabulary to describe the struggle that I had since year 1. I came from a similar background as you. I spent 15 years studying in the same international school in Thailand, ended up getting accepted into one of the top universities in Taiwan for my program, and also getting a government scholarship. Suffice to say, I was confident in my academics, extracurriculars, and my place in a larger community. It all came crashing down when I came to Taiwan. Due to my Chinese heritage, my Taiwanese classmates weren't able to discern me visually from local students - until I opened my mouth to speak. Despite being taught to read, speak, write, and understand Mandarin from the school that I spent 15 years of my life in, I wasn't able to understand certain cultural references nor pick up a "Taiwanese" accent.

Although I am (generally) accepted by the some local students here and wasn't subjected to the treatment that you discussed, I always felt there was a fine line drawn between overseas Chinese and local students. I've always had a hard time to describe it. Maybe it's due to differences in academics, culture, and languages, but I have come around to accept it as part of the studying abroad experience. It's an adjustment.

Thank you so much for sharing. It means the world to know that us international students are not alone.

text:
There's always a way! Even if you can't get into Yonsei you can do study abroad semesters/summer semesters/years in college! Since you are still young you can look up scholarships and apply to as many as u can! The earlier the better! I think it is possible! I think there might be some study-abroad options for high schoolers too but I don't know much about them. I wish you the very best! You can do this!

And for study tips, I don't know what your situation is exactly but for me what worked is if you can spend time in libraries and do Pomodro (which works for me haha) for maybe 2-3 hours every day you could definitely get good grades! I did some asynchronous college courses from a program in high school and would spend 4 hours in the library every day and finish the entire week's worth of homework + learn the content by Wednesday of the same week. Then you could make flashcards as you go and then have study material before quizzes. 

If you can't go to the library try having a consistent study schedule that is realistic (and small enough to where you do it) and getting noise-canceling headphones/headphones with brown noise on to drown the noise out it might help. 

For classes, there are different study methods like 
chemistry/math -- (my organic chemistry tutor on YouTube & other youtube tutorials) + whiteboards OR just normal paper where you redo the questions over and over and over again until you memorize how to do it
History/Health/Biology courses -- notes + make flashcard questions to EVERY section + draw out pictures and mind-maps of concepts

I HIGHLY recommend using Google Calendar to time-block your schedule as realistic as possible. Make sure that you have a specific end-time so it doesn't feel like you are studying forever + it's a motivation to finish your work before the time ends. It's genuinely how everyone I know stays sane as pre-med students haha. 

These are honestly very vague things that helped me and might not work for you but I feel very confident that you can get the grades you want and you can get to Yonsei University and/or become a lawyer! (and a quick google search about studying in abusive households is trying to stay away from home as long as possible -- hopefully in libraries or maybe cafes) I hope the best for you! You should not have to be in this situation as a 14-year-old old and I love the motivation you have 🥺 You can do it!

text:
한국에서 생활하시느라 너무 힘드셨군요. 수많은 외국인이 찾아오지만 결국 적응하는 사람들은 소수에 불과하죠. 

극단적인 날씨와 기후차이(흑서기와 흑한기,  한국의 몬순기와 건조기),  공기오염(국내적 요인과 지정학적 외부적 요인),  북위권과는 차이가 큰 일조량,  가치관의 괴리에서 오는 차이가 큰 음식문화, 사고방식의 차이에서 기인되는 인간관계와 사회문화, 

특히 아직 발전중에 있으나 잠재적으로 남아있는 열악한 전근대적 집단주의적 관념 속 사생활이 침해될 수도 있는 압박감이 군데군데 존재하며, 

그로인해  개인의 반경이 약간이라도 희생되거나 침해되더라도 모두를 위해 상관없다라는 느낌의 서구적인  개인주의가 전무한 시민의식, 주류에 수렴하는데 있어서 일절의 오차도 허용되지 않고 

바로 배척되는 각자의 개성이 존중되지 않는 극단적이며 획일적 소속감에 밀려오는 압박감, 

혹시라도 집단에서 이탈될까봐 늘 긴장하며  자신의 정체성과 생각을 숨기고 눈치를 봐야하는 환경에서의 피로도 등등, 

한국사람들은 그 환경에서 태어나 자라왔고 그런 환경에서 살아갈 수 있도록 교육받고 적응해왔기 떄문에  대부분의 경우 본인들이 처한 환경을 무리하게 변화시키거나 개척하기보다는 주어진 환경에 맞게 만족하거나 , 

만족을 못하더라도 내면적  인내심을 가지며 살아가지만  외국인들의 입장에서는 경우에 따라 불편하고 마음에 상처를 주기도 하겠습니다.  

 물론 외국인 뿐만 아니라 한국인 조차도 이런  환경에 사회적 어느 개체가 감당하는  인내가  한계에 도달하면서  과열되면  치명적인 염증을 겪기도 합니다. 

 못참으면  "화병" 또는 너무 참아버리면  "한" 이라는 한국특유의  개념으로 후유증이 존재하죠. 특히 "화병" 이란 단어는  변경되지 않는 한국어 그대로  질병의 이름으로써  한시적으로 국제 의학학술적 용어로 지정되기도 했죠.(국제 의학계에서 한국의 문화에 관련된 특유한 질환으로 이를 "hwa-byung",  자세히 들여다 보면  alexithymia(감정표현불능증)가 신체화한 질병으로 등재하였다. 인내가 미덕인 유교 문화권에서 발생한다고 보고 있다.)

어쨌던 잘 버텨내셨고 미래에 닥칠지도 모르는 고난을 이겨내는데 한국의 경험이 일종의 하드트레이닝이 됐다면 좋겠습니다. 부디 어느곳에서나 건강하시고 행복하세요. 안녕.
